This matters because adenoma (linked to OCP/steroids) risks bleeding and malignant transformation.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What imaging features are diagnostic of HCC in a cirrhotic liver (LI-RADS), and why is this important?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Arterial-phase hyperenhancement plus portal-venous/delayed washout and an enhancing capsule. In an at-risk (cirrhotic) liver this combination is diagnostic of HCC on imaging alone — no biopsy needed.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Which is the commonest malignant liver lesion overall, and its typical MRI appearance?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Metastases. Often multiple; colorectal mets are typically hypovascular with peripheral rim enhancement and restricted diffusion. Hepatobiliary-phase imaging improves detection of small deposits.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: On liver MRI, what does restricted diffusion (on DWI) suggest, and what MRI safety caution applies to gadolinium?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Restricted diffusion favours malignancy (dense, cellular tissue). Gadolinium should be used with caution in severe renal impairment (historic risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), alongside standard MRI safety screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: On chemical shift MRI, on which image does fat-containing liver lose signal, and why?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: On the OUT-of-phase image (shorter TE at 1.5T). Fat and water protons precess at different frequencies; at the out-of-phase echo their signals cancel, so a voxel containing both loses signal. Produces the India-ink/etching artefact at fat-water interfaces.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What is PDFF and what is it used for?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Proton density fat fraction — a quantitative % of liver fat derived from a multi-echo Dixon sequence. Used to grade and monitor steatosis in NAFLD/MASLD non-invasively (and as a clinical-trial endpoint), replacing biopsy for fat assessment.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: How does iron affect liver MRI signal and how is it quantified?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Iron is paramagnetic and shortens T2*/T2, so an iron-loaded liver loses signal as TE lengthens (darkest on longer-echo/in-phase images). T2*/R2* mapping (R2* = 1/T2*) is calibrated to liver iron concentration (LIC) to guide venesection or chelation.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: State the key opposite behaviour of fat vs iron on chemical shift MRI.
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Fat loses signal on the OUT-of-phase (shorter TE) image; iron loses signal on the IN-phase (longer TE) image. "Fat out, iron in."

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Name the systemic complications of hereditary haemochromatosis that MRI-guided de-ironing aims to prevent.
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Cirrhosis (and HCC), diabetes ("bronze diabetes"), cardiomyopathy, arthropathy and hypogonadism. Usually HFE C282Y homozygosity; quantifying LIC and venesecting before organ damage is disease-modifying.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: On MRI chemical shift imaging, what does a lipid-rich adrenal adenoma do on out-of-phase images compared with in-phase?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: It loses (drops) signal on out-of-phase images because of its intracytoplasmic (microscopic) lipid — fat and water protons within the same voxel cancel. Signal drop confirms a benign lipid-rich adenoma needing no further characterisation follow-up.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: An adrenal lesion shows NO signal drop on out-of-phase imaging. What does this mean?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: It is lipid-poor and therefore indeterminate — not automatically malignant. Differential: lipid-poor adenoma (~30% of adenomas), phaeochromocytoma, metastasis, or adrenocortical carcinoma. Proceed to CT washout and/or hormonal work-up.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What are the two core questions to answer for every adrenal incidentaloma?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: 1) Is it functioning? — biochemistry: cortisol/dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's), aldosterone:renin (Conn's), plasma/urinary metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma). 2) Is it benign or malignant? — imaging: size/morphology plus CT washout or MRI chemical shift.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What is the classic MRI signature of a phaeochromocytoma, and which biochemical test confirms it?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Markedly T2-hyperintense 'light-bulb bright' mass, avidly enhancing, often with cystic/necrotic areas and no out-of-phase drop. Confirmed by elevated plasma/urinary metanephrines.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Why must you never biopsy or operate on an unblocked phaeochromocytoma, and what is the correct pre-operative preparation?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Biopsy/surgery/contrast can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis from catecholamine surge. Prepare with alpha-blockade first, then add beta-blockade — never beta before alpha (unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction).

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Why is MR enterography preferred over CT for imaging small-bowel Crohn's disease, especially in young patients?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: It uses no ionising radiation, so it can be repeated safely across a lifetime of monitoring. It also gives excellent soft-tissue contrast to distinguish active inflammation from fibrosis and assesses transmural/extraluminal disease beyond the colonoscope's reach.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Outline the MR enterography technique (luminal prep and IV agents).
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Large-volume oral mannitol/water solution to distend the bowel (biphasic: T2 bright, T1 dark); IV antiperistaltic agent (hyoscine butylbromide/Buscopan or glucagon) to reduce motion; IV gadolinium for mucosal hyperenhancement; core sequences T2 (±fat sat), T1 pre/post gadolinium, and DWI.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: List the MRE features of ACTIVE inflammation in Crohn's disease.
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Mural thickening (>3 mm), mucosal hyperenhancement post-gadolinium, mural oedema (T2 bright), DWI restriction, the comb sign (engorged vasa recta), and (chronicity marker) fibrofatty proliferation / creeping fat. Classic site: terminal ileum, with skip lesions.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: How does MRE distinguish an inflammatory stricture from a fibrotic one, and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Inflammatory: wall enhancement, T2 oedema, DWI restriction — treat medically (biologics/steroids). Fibrotic: fixed narrowing with little enhancement, low T2 signal, no oedema — won't respond to drugs, may need surgery or endoscopic dilatation. Strictures are often mixed.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What is the comb sign on MR enterography?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Engorged, closely spaced vasa recta radiating perpendicular to an inflamed bowel loop, resembling the teeth of a comb. It reflects mesenteric hyperaemia and indicates active inflammation.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What is the single most important MRI feature that distinguishes a malignant from a benign renal cyst (Bosniak system)?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Enhancement of the septa, walls, or a nodular soft-tissue component after gadolinium. Enhancing thick/irregular septa = Bosniak III; an enhancing soft-tissue nodule = Bosniak IV — both are surgical and likely malignant.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Why is MRI the key modality for local staging of renal cell carcinoma?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: It defines the extent of venous tumour thrombus in the renal vein and IVC — particularly the cranial extent (infrahepatic vs retrohepatic vs supradiaphragmatic/atrial) — which dictates the surgical approach. It also assesses perinephric and nodal spread without radiation or iodinated contrast.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: How does MRI diagnose an angiomyolipoma, and what is the main clinical risk?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: AML contains macroscopic fat, which loses signal on fat-suppressed sequences and shows India-ink boundary artefact on chemical-shift (opposed-phase) imaging. Large AMLs (>4 cm) risk spontaneous haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome); multiple bilateral AMLs suggest tuberous sclerosis.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What are the two main roles of MRI in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: 1) Measuring total kidney volume — the key imaging prognostic marker for disease progression. 2) MRA screening for intracranial berry aneurysms in patients with a relevant family history or symptoms.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: What gadolinium-related risk is especially relevant in renal MRI patients, and who is at risk?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) — associated with gadolinium-based contrast in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) and dialysis patients. Avoid or use macrocyclic (group II) agents and weigh the indication carefully.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: Which focal liver lesions are benign and need no treatment or follow-up?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: A simple cyst (anechoic/CSF-signal), a haemangioma (T2 light-bulb, peripheral nodular fill-in) and focal nodular hyperplasia (central scar retaining hepatobiliary contrast) are benign with no malignant potential — no resection or surveillance. A hepatic adenoma is different: stop the oestrogen (OCP) and resect if >5 cm, male, or growing (haemorrhage/malignancy risk).

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.front: How does MRI chemical-shift imaging characterise an adrenal incidentaloma, and what is the management rule?
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.back: A lipid-rich adenoma loses signal on opposed-phase images (India-ink drop); a lipid-poor metastasis/phaeochromocytoma/carcinoma does not drop. Management: a non-functioning, benign-appearing adenoma <4 cm can be discharged; a functioning lesion, one >4 cm, or an indeterminate/suspicious one is referred for resection (and phaeo excluded biochemically first).

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Which imaging test is the MOST sensitive for breast cancer, and what is its main role?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Contrast-enhanced (dynamic gadolinium) breast MRI. It is used for annual surveillance of high-risk women, in whom mammography alone is inadequate — especially young women with dense breasts.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Name the high-risk groups eligible for annual breast MRI screening (per NICE).
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Known BRCA1/BRCA2 carriers (and untested first-degree relatives), TP53/Li-Fraumeni, other strong family history / high lifetime risk, and women with prior chest/mantle radiotherapy (e.g. Hodgkin lymphoma survivors).

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Why do breast cancers enhance on gadolinium MRI, and what dynamic curve is suspicious?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Cancers are angiogenic with leaky neovasculature, causing rapid avid enhancement. A type 3 curve (rapid uptake then washout) is the classic suspicious/malignant pattern; lesions are categorised with BI-RADS.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: What is the key limitation of breast MRI compared with mammography?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Lower specificity — benign enhancement causes false positives, more recalls and biopsies, plus higher cost, need for contrast, and MRI safety issues. Usually used alongside mammography.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: When in the menstrual cycle should breast MRI be timed, and why?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Days 7–14 (follicular phase) to minimise background parenchymal enhancement, which improves lesion detection and reduces false positives.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: How is breast cancer diagnosed, and where does MRI fit?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Diagnosis is by triple assessment (clinical exam + mammography/US + core biopsy). MRI does not make the diagnosis — once cancer is confirmed it is a selective local-staging / problem-solving tool for surgical planning.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: List the main indications for breast MRI in a diagnosed cancer.
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Assessing disease extent and multifocality/multicentricity (ipsilateral or contralateral additional cancers); invasive lobular carcinoma (often mammographically occult/underestimated); chest wall/pectoral involvement; monitoring neoadjuvant chemotherapy response; occult primary with axillary nodal metastasis; imaging–clinical size discrepancy.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Why is MRI used selectively rather than routinely for all breast cancers?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: It is highly sensitive but only moderately specific, so it overestimates extent and detects incidental benign enhancement — leading to more biopsies and potentially more extensive surgery/mastectomy without a proven survival benefit.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: An MRI finds an unexpected additional enhancing lesion. What must happen before surgery is escalated?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: It must be histologically confirmed (typically second-look ultrasound plus targeted core biopsy). Do not convert to mastectomy on MRI enhancement alone — benign enhancement is common.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: What safety and preparation points apply to contrast breast MRI?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Uses IV gadolinium — check eGFR (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk in severe renal impairment). Standard MRI safety screening (pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, metallic foreign bodies). Prone with breast coils; ideally days 7–14 of cycle in premenopausal women to reduce background enhancement.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: What is the classic MRI sign of INTRACAPSULAR silicone implant rupture, and what does it represent?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: The linguine sign — multiple wavy, low-signal curvilinear lines representing the collapsed silicone shell floating within silicone, while the fibrous capsule remains intact.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: How does intracapsular rupture differ from extracapsular rupture?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Intracapsular: shell ruptures but silicone stays contained within the intact fibrous capsule. Extracapsular: silicone escapes beyond the fibrous capsule into breast tissue/lymph nodes, forming free silicone/siliconomas.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Are radial folds a sign of rupture on breast implant MRI?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: No — radial folds are normal infoldings of the shell into the gel. Do not mistake them for the linguine sign. Silicone tracking into a fold (keyhole/teardrop/noose sign) is an early sign of rupture.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: What contrast and sequences are needed to assess silicone implant integrity on MRI?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: No IV contrast is needed for integrity assessment. Silicone-specific (silicone-selective / water-suppressed) sequences are used to distinguish silicone from water/fat.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: How does BIA-ALCL present and how is it investigated?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma, linked to textured implants; presents with a late (>1 year) peri-implant seroma or mass. Aspirate the fluid and send for cytology and CD30.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: A woman has an axillary node showing ER/PR and GATA3-positive adenocarcinoma, but mammography and ultrasound are normal. What is the diagnosis and next test?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Occult breast primary. Next test is contrast-enhanced breast MRI, which detects the mammographically/US-occult primary in the majority of such cases.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: Which immunohistochemical markers on a nodal metastasis suggest a breast origin?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: ER (oestrogen receptor), PR (progesterone receptor) and GATA3 positivity; HER2 status is also assessed. This breast phenotype prompts breast MRI when conventional imaging is negative.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: How does finding the occult primary on MRI change management?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: It allows breast-conserving surgery and targeted therapy instead of empirical whole-breast radiotherapy or mastectomy given for an unknown primary, and improves staging and adjuvant planning.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: After breast MRI identifies a candidate lesion, how is it sampled?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Second-look (targeted) ultrasound of the enhancing area with US-guided biopsy if seen; if sonographically occult, MRI-guided biopsy with placement of a marker clip for surgical localisation.

investigations__MRI__Breast.front: What safety checks are needed before gadolinium-enhanced breast MRI?
investigations__MRI__Breast.back: Check renal function (avoid high-risk gadolinium agents in severe renal impairment due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), screen for MRI-incompatible implants/devices, ask about pregnancy, and ideally scan in cycle days 7-14 to reduce background enhancement.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What physical principle makes standard intracranial (TOF) MRA work, and does it need contrast?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Time-of-flight relies on FLOW: stationary tissue is saturated (dark) by repeated RF pulses, while fresh inflowing (unsaturated) blood is bright. The flow-related high signal produces the angiogram — NO gadolinium is required.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Where do berry (saccular) aneurysms characteristically arise?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: At arterial branch points of the Circle of Willis — most commonly the anterior communicating artery, the posterior communicating artery, and the middle cerebral artery bifurcation.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Who is offered elective MRA aneurysm screening?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), those with a strong family history (typically ≥2 affected first-degree relatives), and surveillance/follow-up after treated subarachnoid haemorrhage or a known aneurysm.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Why is MRA NOT the first-line angiographic test in acute subarachnoid haemorrhage?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Acute SAH is imaged by non-contrast CT head first; the angiographic work-up is CT angiography (fast, sensitive for aneurysm) and/or digital subtraction angiography (DSA — gold standard and the platform for coiling). MRA is reserved for elective screening/follow-up.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Give a key interpretive pitfall of TOF-MRA.
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: It OVERESTIMATES stenosis: turbulent or slow flow causes signal loss (dephasing), making a narrowing look tighter or a near-occlusion look complete. It is also motion-sensitive. Confirm with CTA/DSA if it will change management.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Which carotid should be assessed for endarterectomy after an ischaemic stroke/TIA, and what grading criteria are used?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: The symptomatic side — the carotid ipsilateral to the ischaemic event. Stenosis is graded by NASCET criteria; ≥50–70% symptomatic stenosis benefits from endarterectomy.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Within what timeframe should carotid endarterectomy be performed after a TIA/stroke?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Urgently — within ~2 weeks of the event, when the benefit in preventing recurrent stroke is greatest.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the 'crescent sign' and what does it indicate?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: A bright crescentic signal in the vessel wall on fat-saturated T1 imaging, from methaemoglobin in an intramural haematoma — the classic sign of carotid or vertebral artery dissection.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Why is arterial dissection an important cause of stroke in young patients?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: It is one of the commonest causes of stroke in the young, arising after neck trauma/manipulation or spontaneously (often with connective tissue disease), and it can present with neck pain, Horner's syndrome and ischaemic symptoms.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: How do TOF-MRA and contrast-enhanced MRA differ for grading carotid stenosis?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: TOF-MRA uses no contrast and depends on flow, so it can overestimate stenosis in turbulent/slow flow. CE-MRA (gadolinium) is faster, less flow-dependent and generally more accurate for grading stenosis.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the key imaging test for suspected cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: MR venography (MRV) — it demonstrates the dural venous sinuses; the diagnostic finding is absent flow / a filling defect in a sinus (commonly superior sagittal, transverse or sigmoid). CT venography is an alternative.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Why is a venous (CVST) infarct distinctive on imaging?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: It does NOT respect arterial territories — it crosses arterial boundaries and is frequently haemorrhagic. A parasagittal haemorrhagic infarct in a young/peripartum patient should trigger MRV.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Name the classic plain-imaging signs of superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Empty delta sign (non-enhancing thrombus surrounded by enhancing dura on contrast) and the cord sign (hyperdense thrombosed vein/sinus on non-contrast CT); also loss of the normal flow void and restricted diffusion on MRI.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the treatment of CVST when there is associated venous haemorrhagic infarction?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Still anticoagulation (therapeutic LMWH or heparin) — you treat the clot; the haemorrhagic infarct is a consequence of venous obstruction and is not a contraindication. Also treat the underlying prothrombotic cause.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Which normal variant can mimic sinus thrombosis on MRV, and how do you avoid over-calling it?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: A hypoplastic or atretic transverse sinus. Look for a correspondingly small bony jugular foramen, absence of thrombus signal, and correlate with plain MRI before diagnosing CVST.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the commonest cause of renal artery stenosis, and where in the artery does it typically sit?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Atherosclerosis (~90% of cases), affecting the ostium/proximal third of the renal artery. Seen in older patients with vascular risk factors.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Which clinical clue after starting an ACE inhibitor/ARB strongly suggests significant (often bilateral) RAS?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: A rise in serum creatinine of more than ~30%. RAAS blockade removes the angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction that was maintaining glomerular filtration pressure.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the classic MRA appearance of fibromuscular dysplasia and who gets it?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: A "string of beads" appearance (alternating stenoses and dilatations) in the mid/distal renal artery, classically in young women. It responds well to balloon angioplasty.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Why is gadolinium contrast a particular concern in patients being imaged for RAS?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Because RAS patients often have significant renal impairment, and gadolinium in severe renal impairment can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF). Non-contrast MRA or alternative imaging may be used.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: Explain the physiology linking RAS to hypertension.
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Reduced perfusion beyond the stenosis triggers juxtaglomerular renin release, activating RAAS. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone causes sodium/water retention, producing renovascular (secondary) hypertension.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What three anatomical levels of peripheral arterial disease does lower-limb MRA run-off classify, and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Aortoiliac, femoropopliteal (commonest = SFA at the adductor hiatus), and infrapopliteal/crural (tibioperoneal). The level and lesion length guide treatment: short focal lesions get angioplasty ± stent, long occlusions get bypass.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What ABPI values indicate PAD, and why can the index be falsely reassuring?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: ABPI <0.9 = PAD (<0.4 suggests critical limb ischaemia). ABPI >1.2 is falsely elevated by incompressible, calcified vessels — typically in diabetes and chronic kidney disease — masking disease in high-risk patients.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: What is the main advantage and the main renal caution of contrast-enhanced MRA?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Advantage: no ionising radiation and no iodinated contrast (good for younger patients and contrast allergy). Caution: gadolinium is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) — check renal function first.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: List the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia and the immediate management.
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis. It is a surgical emergency: give IV heparin and arrange urgent revascularisation — do NOT delay for MRA.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.front: For acute aortic dissection or a ruptured/suspected AAA, why is CT preferred over MRA?
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.back: CT angiography is faster and more readily available in the emergency setting. MRA can show the intimal flap (true vs false lumen) or size an aneurysm, but is too slow for acute, unstable presentations.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Which mpMRI sequence is most important for detecting peripheral-zone prostate cancer?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with the ADC map — cancer restricts diffusion (high signal on high-b DWI, low signal on ADC). DWI is the dominant scoring sequence in the peripheral zone.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How does prostate cancer appear on T2-weighted MRI in the peripheral zone?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: As a rounded/lentiform focus of LOW T2 signal against the normally high-signal peripheral zone.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What does the PI-RADS score represent and what threshold prompts biopsy?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: PI-RADS v2.1 grades 1 (very low) to 5 (very high) the likelihood of clinically significant cancer. A score of ≥3–4 usually prompts a targeted MRI-fusion biopsy.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What local staging features does prostate mpMRI look for, and why?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Extracapsular extension, seminal vesicle invasion, and neurovascular bundle involvement — they guide nerve-sparing surgery versus radiotherapy at MDT.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How do prostate bone metastases appear and how are they assessed?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Typically sclerotic (osteoblastic); assessed with a bone scan or whole-body MRI rather than pelvic mpMRI alone.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What are the classic MRI signal and morphology features of a uterine fibroid (leiomyoma)?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: A well-defined, sharply-marginated mass of LOW (dark) T2 signal, clearly demarcated from adjacent myometrium. MRI is used to count, size and locate them (submucosal, intramural, subserosal, pedunculated) to plan myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How does MRI distinguish adenomyosis from a fibroid?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Adenomyosis is DIFFUSE: junctional-zone thickening >12 mm with small T2-bright foci and an ill-defined, globular ('boggy') uterus. A fibroid is a FOCAL, sharply-marginated discrete dark-T2 mass. Adenomyosis presents with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea and a tender bulky uterus.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What are the MRI signal characteristics of an endometrioma ('chocolate cyst')?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: T1 HYPERINTENSE (from old blood products) that does NOT suppress on fat-saturated sequences (unlike a dermoid), with dependent 'T2 shading'. This confirms haemorrhagic endometriotic content.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Which anatomical sites does MRI map in deep infiltrating endometriosis before surgery?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, bladder and bowel wall — seen as T2-dark fibrotic nodules with tethering and anatomical distortion. MRI defines depth plus ureteric/bowel involvement for MDT surgical planning.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: On MRI, how do you tell a septate uterus from a bicornuate uterus, and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Septate uterus: NORMAL convex/flat fundal outer contour with an internal fibrous septum (correctable hysteroscopically). Bicornuate uterus: external fundal cleft >1 cm indenting the outer contour. The distinction changes fertility management and surgical approach.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Which MRI sequence and feature best demonstrate a cervical tumour, and what is the key sign of parametrial invasion?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: T2-weighted imaging: intermediate/high-signal tumour against the low-signal fibrous cervical stroma. Parametrial invasion is shown by disruption/loss of the low-signal stromal ring with tumour extending into parametrial fat — this shifts management from surgery to chemoradiotherapy.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is the single most important MRI measurement in endometrial cancer, and why?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Depth of myometrial invasion — <50% vs ≥50%. It is the key prognostic/staging factor and guides whether pelvic lymphadenectomy is performed, since ≥50% (deep) invasion carries higher nodal risk.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Why is MRI the preferred modality for local staging of cervical and endometrial cancer?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Superior soft-tissue contrast allows accurate assessment of tumour size, depth of invasion (stromal/myometrial), parametrial, vaginal, bladder/rectal and cervical involvement, and pelvic nodes. FIGO staging now incorporates imaging/surgical findings.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How does MRI complement other investigations in the gynae-oncology pathway?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: MRI gives local staging; it complements EUA (clinical extent), biopsy/hysteroscopy or colposcopy (tissue diagnosis), TVUS (first-line for PMB), and CT/PET-CT (distant metastatic and nodal disease). All feed the MDT.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: A postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. What is the mandatory concern and initial workup?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Investigate with transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial thickness) and endometrial biopsy/hysteroscopy. Never dismiss postmenopausal bleeding.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Why is MRI the gold standard for rectal cancer staging, and what decision does it drive?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: High-resolution MRI gives the best LOCAL staging — depth of invasion (T), nodal status, EMVI, and the tumour's distance from the mesorectal fascia (CRM). It directly decides whether the patient needs neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before TME surgery to achieve a clear margin.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is the mesorectal fascia (MRF) and what does it become at surgery?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: The MRF is the thin fascial envelope around the fatty mesorectum. It is the plane of dissection in total mesorectal excision (TME), so it becomes the circumferential resection margin (CRM). Tumour/node/deposit ≤1 mm from the MRF = threatened/involved CRM → neoadjuvant therapy.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Define the T-stages of rectal cancer on MRI.
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: T1/T2 = confined to the rectal wall (submucosa/muscularis propria intact). T3 = tumour extends through muscularis propria into perirectal fat (substaged by depth). T4 = invades adjacent organs (T4b) or breaches the peritoneal surface (T4a).

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is EMVI and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Extramural venous invasion — tumour extending along and expanding a perirectal vein beyond the muscularis. It is an independent poor prognostic marker (higher risk of distant metastasis) and often supports neoadjuvant treatment.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How are lymph nodes assessed on rectal MRI, and how is distant disease staged?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Nodes are judged by morphology over size: irregular/spiculated border, mixed heterogeneous signal, and round shape are suspicious. Distant metastases (liver, lung) are staged by CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, not by pelvic MRI.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for pre-operative mapping of a perianal fistula?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: MRI pelvis using a dedicated anal fistula protocol — it maps the primary tract, its relationship to the sphincter complex, secondary tracts/abscesses and the internal opening, reducing recurrence and incontinence from missed tracts.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: List the four Parks classification types of anal fistula.
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Intersphincteric (commonest), transsphincteric, suprasphincteric and extrasphincteric — classified by the tract's relationship to the anal sphincters.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: On MRI, how does an active fistula tract appear on T2/STIR and post-gadolinium sequences?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Bright (high signal) fluid within the tract on T2/STIR, with enhancing granulation tissue lining the wall after gadolinium. A fibrotic/inactive tract is dark and enhances little.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Why does the amount of sphincter a tract crosses matter surgically?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: It determines whether the tract can be laid open (fistulotomy) safely or needs a sphincter-preserving technique (seton, LIFT, advancement flap) to avoid faecal incontinence.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: Which inflammatory bowel disease is strongly associated with complex/multiple perianal fistulae, and how is it managed?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Crohn's disease (perianal Crohn's) — produces complex, branching or multiple tracts and needs a combined medical (biologics/immunomodulators) and surgical MDT approach with conservative surgery such as setons.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is the role of MRI in assessing an ovarian/adnexal mass, and when is it used?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: MRI is the best problem-solving test for characterising an INDETERMINATE adnexal mass after ultrasound (first-line). It uses tissue signatures (fat, blood, fibrous tissue) plus dynamic contrast enhancement, reported via the O-RADS MRI risk system, to sort masses into benign vs malignant and guide gynae-oncology referral.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: How do a dermoid (mature cystic teratoma) and an endometrioma differ on fat-saturated MRI?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Both are T1 hyperintense. A dermoid contains macroscopic FAT, so its bright T1 signal DROPS on fat-sat/chemical-shift imaging (may have a Rokitansky nodule). An endometrioma is bright due to BLOOD, so it does NOT suppress on fat-sat and shows low-signal 'T2 shading'.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What MRI signature identifies an ovarian fibroma/fibrothecoma, and what syndrome may it cause?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: A solid mass that is VERY LOW signal on T2 (dense fibrous tissue). It is benign but may cause Meigs syndrome — the triad of ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion, which resolves after tumour removal.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: List the MRI features that favour a malignant (epithelial ovarian) cancer.
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: Large size; solid/vascular components with avid enhancement; thick irregular enhancing septa and papillary projections; necrosis; and signs of spread — ascites, peritoneal deposits, and omental cake. These raise the O-RADS MRI score toward high malignancy probability.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.front: What is the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) and what are its three components?
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.back: RMI is a clinical score used alongside imaging to triage referral of an ovarian mass. RMI = US features score × Menopausal status × serum CA-125. A raised RMI prompts referral to the gynae-oncology MDT.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Which whole-body sequences are combined in WB-MRI for myeloma/metastasis imaging?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: T1, STIR, and whole-body diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). Tumour marrow is dark on T1 and bright on STIR / high-b DWI.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why has WB-MRI replaced the skeletal survey as first-line whole-body imaging for suspected myeloma (NICE)?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: It is far more sensitive for marrow disease — detecting focal lesions and diffuse infiltration before any lytic destruction is visible on plain X-ray.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What MRI finding distinguishes active from smouldering myeloma?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: The presence of >=1 unequivocal focal marrow lesion on MRI is a myeloma-defining event indicating active (treatment-requiring) myeloma.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why is a radionuclide bone scan falsely negative in multiple myeloma?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Myeloma is purely lytic/osteoclastic with little reactive bone formation; bone scans detect osteoblastic activity, so myeloma lesions produce little or no tracer uptake.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: How does marrow signal change when tumour replaces normal fatty marrow?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Normal fatty marrow is bright on T1; tumour replacement makes it dark on T1 and bright on STIR and high-b DWI.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: On DWI and ADC, what does TRUE restricted diffusion look like?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Bright (high signal) on DWI AND dark (low signal) on the ADC map. Both must agree — this confirms real restriction (e.g. acute infarct, abscess, hypercellular tumour).

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why is DWI the key sequence in acute stroke?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Cytotoxic oedema (Na+/K+ pump failure, cells swell) restricts water diffusion. DWI is the earliest and most sensitive sign, positive within minutes — hours before CT or T2/FLAIR change. Infarct is bright DWI, dark ADC.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What is T2 shine-through and how do you avoid the trap?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: A strongly T2-bright lesion appears bright on DWI without true restriction (DWI is T2-based). Confirm with the ADC map: true restriction is dark ADC; shine-through has bright/normal ADC.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: How does DWI distinguish a cerebral abscess from a necrotic tumour?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: The viscous, cellular pus in an abscess RESTRICTS diffusion — bright DWI, dark ADC in the cavity. The necrotic core of a tumour does not restrict. This is a classic discriminator.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Give two uses of DWI beyond acute stroke.
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Oncology: detecting hypercellular lesions (metastases, lymphoma, myeloma on whole-body DWI), characterising benign vs malignant tissue, and assessing treatment response (rising ADC = falling cellularity). Needs no contrast.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What signal does fMRI measure and what does it stand for?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: The BOLD signal — Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent. It is an indirect, haemodynamic marker of neuronal activity based on the changing ratio of oxy- to deoxy-haemoglobin in active brain regions.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why do the magnetic properties of haemoglobin matter in fMRI?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic (minimal field distortion) whereas deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic (distorts the field, lowering signal). Neuronal activity increases local blood flow, delivering excess oxyhaemoglobin and washing out deoxyhaemoglobin, so the T2*-weighted signal rises and the region 'lights up'.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What is the main clinical use of fMRI?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Pre-surgical planning — mapping eloquent cortex (motor, sensory and language areas such as Broca's/Wernicke's) adjacent to a brain tumour or epileptic focus so the surgeon avoids causing post-operative neurological deficits. It also lateralises language/memory as an adjunct/alternative to the Wada test.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Task-based vs resting-state fMRI — what's the difference?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Task-based: the patient performs a task (e.g. finger tapping for motor cortex, word generation for language) and activation is contrasted against rest. Resting-state: no task; spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations reveal functional connectivity/intrinsic networks — useful when the patient cannot cooperate.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: List key limitations of fMRI.
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Indirect (haemodynamic, not direct neuronal recording); lower temporal resolution (BOLD lags neural activity by seconds); highly motion-sensitive; task paradigms need patient cooperation; specialised rather than a routine clinical test; and standard MRI safety/screening constraints apply.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Is fetal MRI a first- or second-line investigation, and what is first-line?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Second-line/problem-solving. Antenatal ULTRASOUND is first-line; MRI is used to further characterise an abnormality US has detected, most often of the fetal brain/CNS.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why is fetal MRI considered safe in pregnancy, and what contrast agent is avoided?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: It uses no ionising radiation. GADOLINIUM is avoided because it crosses the placenta into the amniotic fluid — fetal MRI is a non-contrast study. Usually performed in the 2nd/3rd trimester.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: How does fetal MRI overcome fetal motion and get tissue contrast?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Fast single-shot T2 sequences acquire each slice almost instantly, "freezing" motion (no sedation needed). Bright amniotic fluid provides natural contrast and T2 gives excellent CSF/grey-white differentiation.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Name common CNS indications for fetal MRI.
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Ventriculomegaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, posterior fossa anomalies (Dandy-Walker), cortical malformations, and neural tube defects/spina bifida with Chiari II (also helps plan fetal or postnatal surgery).

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Which non-CNS findings on fetal MRI change delivery planning?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Airway-threatening neck mass (plan an EXIT procedure), severe congenital diaphragmatic hernia (lung volume/prognosis), and placenta accreta spectrum (massive haemorrhage risk) — all need fetal-medicine MDT management.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What physical property of water diffusion does DTI measure, and how does this differ from standard diffusion imaging?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: DTI measures the directionality (anisotropy) of water diffusion — not just whether diffusion is restricted, but which way water moves. In white-matter tracts water diffuses preferentially along the axon bundles (anisotropic), which DTI models as a tensor at each voxel to reconstruct 3D tracts (tractography).

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: In DTI colour-coded fibre maps, what does each of red, green and blue represent?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: Red = left–right (transverse, e.g. corpus callosum); Green = anterior–posterior; Blue = superior–inferior (cranio-caudal, e.g. corticospinal tracts). Colour encodes the principal direction of diffusion at that voxel.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What is Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and how is a reduced FA interpreted?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: FA is a scalar (0–1) quantifying how directional diffusion is — a marker of tract integrity. High FA = organised, intact tracts; reduced FA suggests tract disruption/damage (e.g. axonal loss or demyelination). It is sensitive but non-specific for the cause.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: Why is DTI/tractography used in neurosurgical planning, and how does it complement fMRI?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: It maps major white-matter tracts (corticospinal, arcuate fasciculus, optic radiations) running around a tumour so the surgeon can preserve them and avoid post-operative deficits. DTI maps the white-matter wiring; fMRI maps grey-matter function — together they define eloquent tissue to protect during resection.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.front: What are the main limitations of DTI?
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.back: It struggles with crossing fibres within a single voxel (the simple tensor model misrepresents them), it is an indirect model-based reconstruction (tracts are inferences, not direct images of axons), and it is specialised and research-heavy — requiring dedicated acquisition and post-processing rather than being a routine sequence.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old presents with sudden right-sided weakness 40 minutes ago. CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. Which MRI sequence would most sensitively confirm an acute ischaemic stroke at this early stage?
options: T1-weighted imaging
T2-weighted imaging
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with ADC map
Gradient echo (GRE/SWI)
Post-gadolinium T1
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with ADC map
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: DWI is the earliest and most sensitive sequence for acute infarction, showing restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) within minutes, long before CT or conventional T1/T2 changes appear. GRE detects blood, and post-gadolinium T1 detects BBB breakdown, neither of which is the earliest stroke sign.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: On an axial brain MRI, the CSF within the lateral ventricles appears bright (high signal) and periventricular white matter lesions are conspicuous, while the CSF signal has been nulled on a companion image. Which pair of sequences is being described?
options: T1 and post-gadolinium T1
DWI and ADC
GRE and SWI
T1 and T2
T2 and FLAIR
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: T2 and FLAIR
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Bright CSF indicates a T2-weighted image (Water is White on T2). FLAIR is a T2 sequence with the CSF signal suppressed (nulled) so periventricular lesions stand out. The described combination of bright-CSF T2 plus a CSF-suppressed companion is therefore T2 and FLAIR.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient is referred for a routine brain MRI. Which finding in the safety screening should most strongly prompt further investigation before entering the scanner?
options: A history of well-controlled hypertension
A history of metal grinding with possible retained intra-orbital metallic fragment
Previous appendicectomy
A titanium dental crown
Mild anxiety about enclosed spaces
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A history of metal grinding with possible retained intra-orbital metallic fragment
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A ferromagnetic intra-orbital foreign body can move within the strong magnetic field and cause globe injury or blindness, so a grinding/metalwork history mandates screening imaging (e.g. orbital radiographs) before MRI. Titanium is non-ferromagnetic and MR-safe; the other options are not MRI hazards.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old presents 90 minutes after sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia. MRI shows a wedge of high signal on DWI in the left hemisphere. Which finding on the ADC map confirms this is TRUE acute diffusion restriction rather than T2 shine-through?
options: High (bright) signal on ADC
No change on ADC
Blooming low signal on GRE
Low (dark) signal on ADC
Ring enhancement on post-contrast imaging
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Low (dark) signal on ADC
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: True acute restriction is DWI bright WITH ADC dark (low). If the ADC were bright/normal, the DWI signal would represent T2 shine-through, not acute cytotoxic restriction. GRE blooming indicates haemorrhage and ring enhancement suggests abscess/tumour.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient wakes with a hemiparesis and cannot say when symptoms began. MRI shows a lesion that is DWI positive but FLAIR negative. What does this DWI–FLAIR mismatch most likely indicate?
options: The stroke onset is likely within the last 4.5 hours
The stroke is more than 24 hours old
The lesion is a chronic infarct
The lesion is haemorrhagic
The lesion represents a tumour rather than infarct
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: The stroke onset is likely within the last 4.5 hours
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: DWI turns positive within minutes while FLAIR lags ~4.5–6 h. DWI+/FLAIR− (mismatch) implies onset is probably <4.5 h, supporting thrombolysis in wake-up or unknown-onset stroke.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which statement about MRI in the hyperacute stroke pathway is CORRECT?
options: MRI should always be performed before CT to save time
DWI is unable to detect posterior fossa infarcts
A non-contrast CT head is done first to exclude haemorrhage so reperfusion is not delayed
GRE/SWI sequences are insensitive to haemorrhage
ADC remains low permanently after infarction
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A non-contrast CT head is done first to exclude haemorrhage so reperfusion is not delayed
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: CT is fast and universally available and reliably excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis; MRI must not delay time-critical reperfusion. DWI is in fact superior for posterior fossa infarcts, GRE/SWI are highly sensitive to blood, and ADC pseudonormalises over days.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A DWI-restricting lesion is seen but the clinical picture is atypical for stroke (fever, no vascular territory pattern). Which of the following is a recognised NON-stroke cause of diffusion restriction?
options: Simple arachnoid cyst
Chronic lacunar scar
Normal choroid plexus
Fat within a dermoid
Cerebral abscess
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Cerebral abscess
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Central pus in a cerebral abscess restricts diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) and shows a ring-enhancing wall; hypercellular tumours (lymphoma, high-grade glioma) can also restrict. These mimics are why lesion shape, enhancement pattern and clinical context matter, not DWI alone.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient has sudden vertigo, ataxia and diplopia; CT brain is reported as normal. Why is MRI-DWI particularly valuable here?
options: CT is more sensitive than MRI for posterior fossa infarcts
MRI-DWI detects small brainstem/cerebellar infarcts that CT often misses due to bone artefact
DWI cannot image the posterior circulation
FLAIR is positive before DWI in the brainstem
MRI is contraindicated in posterior circulation stroke
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: MRI-DWI detects small brainstem/cerebellar infarcts that CT often misses due to bone artefact
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: CT of the posterior fossa is degraded by beam-hardening/bone artefact, so small brainstem and cerebellar infarcts are frequently missed. DWI is highly sensitive there, making it the test of choice for posterior circulation symptoms with a normal CT.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 29-year-old woman has an episode of painful visual loss in one eye that recovered. MRI brain FLAIR shows several ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the corpus callosum, plus a juxtacortical lesion. Post-gadolinium imaging shows one lesion enhances while the others do not. Which statement best explains why MS can be diagnosed from this single scan?
options: Optic neuritis alone is diagnostic of MS
The perpendicular orientation of lesions is pathognomonic and sufficient
Any white-matter lesion on FLAIR confirms demyelination
Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions satisfy dissemination in time, and ≥2 typical sites satisfy dissemination in space
Enhancement excludes MS because it indicates infection
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions satisfy dissemination in time, and ≥2 typical sites satisfy dissemination in space
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: McDonald criteria require dissemination in space (≥2 of the four typical locations — here periventricular + juxtacortical) and in time. An enhancing lesion coexisting with a non-enhancing lesion demonstrates lesions of differing age on one scan, satisfying DIT without a follow-up study.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which MRI feature would most strongly suggest an alternative diagnosis rather than typical multiple sclerosis?
options: A longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion spanning several vertebral segments
Short-segment peripheral cervical cord lesion
Ovoid periventricular lesions on sagittal FLAIR
A juxtacortical lesion touching the cortex
An open-ring enhancing white-matter lesion
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion spanning several vertebral segments
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: MS cord lesions are characteristically short (<2 vertebral bodies) and peripheral. A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis lesion points instead to neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibody), a red flag against typical MS. The other features are all typical of MS.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: What does gadolinium enhancement of a white-matter plaque on T1 imaging indicate in multiple sclerosis?
options: Chronic axonal loss (a 'black hole')
Small-vessel ischaemic change
Active demyelination with blood–brain barrier breakdown
Cerebral atrophy
An artefact from CSF suppression on FLAIR
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Active demyelination with blood–brain barrier breakdown
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Gadolinium cannot cross an intact blood–brain barrier. In acute demyelination the BBB is disrupted, allowing contrast to leak into the lesion, so enhancement marks an active/acute plaque (usually for ~2–6 weeks). Non-enhancing lesions are old; black holes reflect chronic axonal loss.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 58-year-old presents with headache and left-arm weakness. MRI+gadolinium shows a solitary intra-axial mass with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis and extensive surrounding T2/FLAIR oedema, crossing the corpus callosum to the contralateral hemisphere. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Meningioma
Cerebral abscess
Acute infarct
Tumefactive multiple sclerosis
Glioblastoma
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Glioblastoma
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Thick irregular ring enhancement with central necrosis, marked vasogenic oedema and midline crossing through the corpus callosum (butterfly appearance) is the classic pattern of glioblastoma. Meningioma is extra-axial with a dural tail; an abscess would show a thin smooth ring with central restricted diffusion; infarct follows a vascular territory; tumefactive MS classically shows an open (incomplete) enhancing ring.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A ring-enhancing lesion is seen on MRI. On diffusion-weighted imaging the centre of the lesion shows marked restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, low ADC). Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
options: Glioblastoma
Cerebral abscess
Solitary metastasis
Radiation necrosis
Meningioma
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Cerebral abscess
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Central restricted diffusion within a ring-enhancing lesion reflects viscous, cellular pus and is the classic feature of a cerebral abscess. Most necrotic tumours (glioblastoma, metastasis) have a non-restricting central cavity. This single sequence critically changes management from biopsy/resection to antibiotics and neurosurgical drainage.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: An MRI shows a well-defined, homogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass with a broad dural base, a dural tail sign and a CSF cleft separating it from the brain. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastasis
Glioblastoma
Cerebral abscess
Meningioma
Low-grade astrocytoma
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Meningioma
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A broad dural base, dural tail sign, CSF cleft and homogeneous avid enhancement are hallmark features of an extra-axial meningioma. Metastases and gliomas are intra-axial (within brain parenchyma) and lack a CSF cleft; an abscess shows a ring with central restricted diffusion. Identifying the extra-axial location first narrows the differential decisively.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 24-year-old with drug-resistant seizures and rising epigastric aura undergoes an epilepsy-protocol MRI. Coronal FLAIR shows a small right hippocampus with high signal and loss of internal architecture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis
Focal cortical dysplasia
Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour (DNET)
Cavernoma
Cortical heterotopia
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Hippocampal atrophy, increased T2/FLAIR signal and loss of internal architecture are the diagnostic triad of hippocampal sclerosis, the commonest substrate of temporal lobe epilepsy and one that is potentially curable with anterior temporal lobectomy. The other options are alternative substrates but do not produce this hippocampal triad.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which sequence and orientation is most important for detecting the commonest surgically-treatable substrate in an epilepsy-protocol MRI?
options: Axial diffusion-weighted imaging through the whole brain
Sagittal T1 volumetric sequence of the midline
Coronal T2/FLAIR angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus
Post-contrast axial T1 of the posterior fossa
Gradient-echo axial imaging of the basal ganglia
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Coronal T2/FLAIR angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Thin-slice coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus allows direct side-to-side comparison and reveals the atrophy and signal change of hippocampal sclerosis that routine axial imaging often misses. The other sequences do not optimally interrogate the mesial temporal structures.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A previously well 55-year-old has a first focal seizure and is found to have a new right-sided pronator drift. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and arrange routine outpatient EEG only
Start lifelong sodium valproate without imaging
Discharge with no follow-up as most first seizures are benign
Repeat clinical review in six months before any investigation
Arrange urgent neuroimaging to exclude a structural lesion such as a tumour
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Arrange urgent neuroimaging to exclude a structural lesion such as a tumour
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A first seizure with a focal neurological deficit is a red flag that may indicate an underlying tumour or other serious structural pathology, so urgent imaging is required rather than reassurance. Driving advice (stop driving, notify the DVLA) and screening for MRI contraindications should also be addressed.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 72-year-old presents with 18 months of memory decline. Coronal T1 MRI shows bilateral medial temporal lobe atrophy with a high Scheltens MTA score and parietotemporal volume loss. Which diagnosis does this best support?
options: Frontotemporal dementia
Alzheimer's disease
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Vascular dementia
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Alzheimer's disease
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Hippocampal/medial temporal lobe atrophy (high MTA score) with parietotemporal involvement is the classic Alzheimer's signature. FTD gives asymmetric frontal/anterior temporal atrophy, DLB relatively spares the medial temporal lobe, NPH shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, and vascular dementia shows small-vessel disease.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old has a gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. MRI shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to cortical atrophy with tight high-convexity sulci. What is the most important reason to recognise this pattern?
options: It confirms irreversible Alzheimer's disease
It is diagnostic of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
It represents normal age-related change
It indicates a potentially shunt-responsive condition
It requires immediate craniotomy
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: It indicates a potentially shunt-responsive condition
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: The triad plus ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy (DESH pattern) is normal pressure hydrocephalus, a treatable/reversible cause of dementia that may respond to CSF shunting — hence the importance of not missing it. CJD is suggested by DWI cortical ribboning, not this pattern.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 59-year-old develops rapidly progressive cognitive decline over weeks with myoclonus. Which MRI sequence and finding would most support Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
options: DWI showing cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion
T1 showing hippocampal atrophy
FLAIR showing confluent white-matter hyperintensities
T2* showing multiple microbleeds
Post-gadolinium showing meningeal enhancement
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: DWI showing cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia should trigger urgent imaging for reversible/serious causes; in CJD, DWI classically shows restricted diffusion as cortical ribboning and in the basal ganglia. Hippocampal atrophy suggests AD, confluent white-matter change suggests small-vessel disease, and microbleeds relate to amyloid/hypertensive angiopathy.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 34-year-old presents with fever, confusion and expressive dysphasia. MRI shows asymmetric FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling of the left medial temporal lobe and insula, sparing the basal ganglia. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Await CSF HSV PCR before starting any treatment
Arrange urgent CT angiogram for stroke thrombolysis
Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately
Start IV dexamethasone alone and observe
Repeat MRI in 48 hours to confirm progression
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: The pattern is classic for HSV encephalitis. Treatment is time-critical and must not wait for PCR or repeat imaging — empirical IV aciclovir is started at once. PCR can be falsely negative early, and delay worsens outcome. Basal ganglia sparing helps distinguish it from MCA infarction, so thrombolysis is inappropriate.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient has a ring-enhancing cerebral lesion with surrounding oedema. Which single MRI feature best supports a pyogenic abscess over a necrotic high-grade tumour?
options: A thick, irregular, nodular enhancing wall
Absence of surrounding vasogenic oedema
Facilitated diffusion in the lesion centre
Homogeneous enhancement of the whole lesion
Central restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC)
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Central restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC)
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Viscous pus in an abscess restricts diffusion centrally — bright on DWI with low ADC — whereas a necrotic tumour core typically does not restrict (facilitated diffusion, high ADC) and has a thicker, more irregular wall. Both may show oedema, so that is not discriminatory.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis has a new focal neurological deficit and reduced GCS. What is the correct sequence of management?
options: Perform lumbar puncture first, then treat based on results
Take blood cultures and give antibiotics, then image before LP
Delay all antibiotics until MRI and LP are both complete
Perform LP immediately regardless of the focal signs
Give antibiotics only after LP confirms bacterial cause
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Take blood cultures and give antibiotics, then image before LP
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Focal deficit, depressed GCS, seizures or signs of raised ICP require imaging before LP to exclude a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus and the risk of coning. However, this must never delay empirical treatment — take blood cultures and give antibiotics (plus aciclovir if encephalitis is possible) first, then image, then LP if safe.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which MRI finding is most characteristic of CNS tuberculosis?
options: Bilateral non-haemorrhagic medial temporal signal only
Solitary periventricular homogeneously enhancing mass
Central restricted diffusion in a thin-walled cystic lesion
Basal leptomeningeal enhancement with tuberculomas and hydrocephalus
Isolated gyral petechial haemorrhage of the frontal lobes
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Basal leptomeningeal enhancement with tuberculomas and hydrocephalus
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: TB meningitis characteristically produces thick basal leptomeningeal enhancement, parenchymal tuberculomas (ring or nodular enhancing), communicating hydrocephalus and infarcts from associated vasculitis. Bilateral medial temporal signal suggests autoimmune/HSV encephalitis; a solitary periventricular enhancing mass suggests lymphoma.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Before an urgent contrast-enhanced MRI brain for suspected CNS infection, which factor is the most important routine safety check?
options: Screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants/foreign bodies
Confirming the patient has fasted for 12 hours
Ensuring the patient can lie prone for the scan
Checking serum sodium before gadolinium
Verifying a normal chest radiograph first
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants/foreign bodies
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: MRI safety screening for ferromagnetic and electronic implants (pacemakers, cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies) is mandatory because the static magnetic field can cause device malfunction or projectile injury. Gadolinium is weighed against renal function (eGFR), not sodium, and fasting/prone positioning are not routine requirements.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient with a dense MCA syndrome at 8 hours has MRI showing a small diffusion core but a large perfusion deficit (mismatch) and a proximal M1 occlusion. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: IV thrombolysis only
Aspirin and admit
Mechanical thrombectomy
No intervention — outside all windows
Decompressive craniectomy
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Mechanical thrombectomy
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A proximal large-vessel occlusion with a small core and large salvageable penumbra (mismatch) can be treated by mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours from onset. Thrombolysis alone is limited to <4.5 h; here thrombectomy is the key intervention.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 68-year-old man develops sudden vertigo, gait ataxia and vomiting. Non-contrast CT head is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat CT head in 24 hours
CT venogram
MRI brain including diffusion-weighted imaging
Lumbar puncture
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Posterior circulation (cerebellar) strokes are frequently missed on early CT due to bone beam-hardening artefact and small lesion size. MRI-DWI detects acute infarction within minutes and is the investigation of choice for the posterior fossa. A normal CT does not exclude a cerebellar stroke.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 55-year-old woman has progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI shows an enhancing cerebellopontine angle mass extending into a widened internal acoustic meatus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Meningioma
Epidermoid cyst
Medulloblastoma
Haemangioblastoma
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma is the commonest CPA lesion and characteristically widens the internal acoustic meatus, giving an "ice-cream cone" appearance with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Meningiomas are centred off the meatus with a dural tail and no meatal expansion; epidermoids show restricted diffusion and follow CSF signal.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 3 cm cerebellar haemorrhage is identified in a drowsy patient. Which complication most directly makes this a neurosurgical emergency?
options: Vasospasm of the basilar artery
Compression of the 4th ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Middle cerebral artery territory infarction
Subfalcine herniation
Cavernous sinus thrombosis
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: Compression of the 4th ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: In the tight posterior fossa, an expanding cerebellar clot compresses the 4th ventricle, obstructing CSF flow and producing acute hydrocephalus with risk of tonsillar/upward coning and brainstem death. This mandates urgent neurosurgical assessment; decompression is considered for clots >3 cm or with brainstem compression or falling GCS.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A teenager has cough-induced occipital headache. Sagittal MRI shows peg-like cerebellar tonsils extending 8 mm below the foramen magnum. Which additional finding should be specifically sought?
options: Bilateral acoustic neuromas
Cerebellar mural nodule with cyst
Dural tail sign
Cervical cord syrinx (syringomyelia)
Restricted diffusion within a CPA cyst
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Tonsillar herniation >5 mm below the foramen magnum defines a Chiari I malformation. It disrupts CSF flow at the craniocervical junction and is classically associated with a cervical cord syrinx, so the whole spinal cord should be imaged. The other options describe schwannoma, haemangioblastoma/pilocytic astrocytoma, meningioma and epidermoid respectively.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to MRI that must be excluded before scanning the posterior fossa?
options: Non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker
Titanium hip prosthesis
Dental amalgam fillings
Recent intravenous cannula
Tattoos on the forearm
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: A non-MRI-conditional pacemaker/ICD is a classic contraindication due to risk of device malfunction and lead heating. Other true contraindications include cochlear implants, intraocular/intracranial metallic foreign bodies and certain ferromagnetic aneurysm clips. Titanium prostheses, dental amalgam and tattoos are generally MRI-safe (tattoos may rarely warm slightly).

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with sudden severe headache, reduced vision and drooping of one eyelid with a dilated pupil. She is hypotensive and drowsy. MRI shows a haemorrhagic sellar mass. What is the most important immediate management step?
options: Urgent transsphenoidal surgery before any medical treatment
Start a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline
Intravenous hydrocortisone for presumed secondary adrenal insufficiency
IV mannitol to reduce intracranial pressure
Lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: Intravenous hydrocortisone for presumed secondary adrenal insufficiency
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: This is pituitary apoplexy. The life-threatening component is secondary adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis), so IV hydrocortisone must be given immediately, ahead of imaging delays or surgery. Endocrine and neurosurgical teams are then involved urgently; surgery may follow but does not precede steroid replacement.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A pituitary macroadenoma extends upward out of the sella. Which structure is compressed to produce the classic bitemporal hemianopia?
options: Optic tract
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery
Oculomotor nerve
Optic chiasm
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Suprasellar extension compresses the optic chiasm, damaging the crossing nasal-retinal fibres that carry the temporal visual fields, giving a bitemporal hemianopia. The optic tract, when affected, produces a homonymous defect, and the cavernous carotid/oculomotor nerve relate to lateral extension, not the field defect.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: Which cranial nerves are at risk when a pituitary macroadenoma invades the cavernous sinus laterally?
options: II only
III, IV, V1, V2 and VI
I, II and VIII
VII and VIII
IX, X, XI and XII
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: The cavernous sinus, lateral to the sella, transmits cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI (along with the internal carotid artery). Lateral tumour extension can therefore cause ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory disturbance. The optic nerve (II) lies above, related to the chiasm, not within the sinus.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A dedicated pituitary MRI is requested for a suspected microadenoma. Which protocol best characterises the lesion?
options: Non-contrast axial CT of the whole brain
Whole-brain FLAIR and diffusion-weighted imaging only
MR angiography of the circle of Willis
Thin-slice coronal and sagittal T1 and T2 through the sella with dynamic gadolinium
Standard 5 mm axial T1 brain sequences without contrast
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: Thin-slice coronal and sagittal T1 and T2 through the sella with dynamic gadolinium
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: A dedicated pituitary study uses thin (~2-3 mm) coronal and sagittal T1 and T2 focused on the sella, with dynamic post-gadolinium imaging. This exploits the slower enhancement of adenomas relative to normal gland to detect small microadenomas that routine thick-slice brain sequences would miss.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 9-year-old presents with growth failure and visual problems. MRI shows a suprasellar cystic and solid mass, and plain imaging shows calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Craniopharyngioma
Prolactinoma
Rathke cleft cyst
Empty sella syndrome
Non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: A suprasellar, mixed cystic/solid, calcified mass in a child is the classic craniopharyngioma, presenting with endocrine (growth) and visual disturbance. Prolactinomas and non-functioning adenomas are typically not calcified, a Rathke cleft cyst is a simple non-enhancing cyst, and empty sella is CSF flattening the gland, not a mass.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 52-year-old presents with 6 months of progressive left-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Pure-tone audiometry shows asymmetric sensorineural loss on the left. What is the single most appropriate investigation?
options: CT temporal bones without contrast
Tympanometry and reflex testing
MRI internal auditory meatus with heavily T2-weighted and post-gadolinium sequences
Repeat audiogram in 12 months
Plain skull radiograph
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: MRI internal auditory meatus with heavily T2-weighted and post-gadolinium sequences
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Unilateral/asymmetric SNHL requires MRI IAM to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. CISS/FIESTA shows a filling defect in the CSF and post-gadolinium T1 shows avid enhancement. It should not be dismissed or merely rescanned by audiogram.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: On a heavily T2-weighted CISS/FIESTA sequence of the IAM, how does a small intracanalicular vestibular schwannoma typically appear?
options: A bright hyperintense mass filling the whole IAM
An area of restricted diffusion with no CSF signal
A calcified lesion with a broad dural base
A flow void within the basilar artery
A dark filling defect replacing the bright CSF around the nerves
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: A dark filling defect replacing the bright CSF around the nerves
