investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: On heavily T2-weighted sequences CSF is bright and the nerves appear as thin dark strands. A schwannoma is a soft-tissue filling defect within that bright CSF; it then enhances avidly on post-gadolinium T1. Restricted diffusion and a broad dural base point to epidermoid and meningioma respectively.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A large cerebellopontine angle mass extends medially and begins to compress adjacent structures. Which additional clinical sign most specifically indicates trigeminal (CN V) involvement?
options: Facial droop with loss of forehead movement
Absent corneal reflex with facial numbness
Nystagmus on lateral gaze
Bilateral papilloedema
Loss of taste on the anterior tongue
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: Absent corneal reflex with facial numbness
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Large CPA lesions compress CN V, producing facial sensory loss and a reduced/absent corneal reflex (V is the afferent limb). Facial droop reflects CN VII (relatively resistant, so a late sign), and papilloedema would reflect raised intracranial pressure from hydrocephalus rather than being CN V-specific.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful loss of vision in her right eye over 3 days, with red desaturation. MRI orbits shows a swollen, enhancing right optic nerve on fat-suppressed post-gadolinium imaging. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Orbital CT with contrast
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Temporal artery biopsy
MRI brain to assess for demyelination
Fluorescein angiography
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: MRI brain to assess for demyelination
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: The picture is optic neuritis, which is strongly associated with multiple sclerosis. An MRI brain looks for periventricular white-matter demyelinating lesions, which predict conversion to MS and guide disease-modifying therapy. The orbital findings alone are already established.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 45-year-old man with Graves disease and proptosis has MRI orbits. Which finding is most characteristic of thyroid eye disease?
options: Enlargement of extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendinous insertions
Enlargement of extraocular muscles including the tendinous insertions
A well-defined enhancing intraconal mass separate from the muscles
'Tram-track' enhancement around the optic nerve
Diffuse enhancement of the lacrimal gland only
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: Enlargement of extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendinous insertions
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Thyroid eye disease enlarges the muscle bellies (worst in inferior and medial recti) while sparing the tendons. Tendon involvement instead suggests orbital myositis. Apical crowding from enlarged muscles risks compressive optic neuropathy.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 40-year-old metalworker who was grinding steel presents with an orbital injury and possible foreign body. Why is MRI contraindicated as the first investigation?
options: MRI cannot image the bony orbit at all
Gadolinium is nephrotoxic in eye injuries
A ferromagnetic intra-orbital foreign body could move in the magnetic field and damage the eye
MRI takes too long in an emergency setting
Fat suppression fails in the presence of blood
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.answer: A ferromagnetic intra-orbital foreign body could move in the magnetic field and damage the eye
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: An intra-orbital ferromagnetic foreign body is a hard contraindication to MRI because the field can displace it and cause catastrophic ocular injury. CT or plain radiographs are used first to screen for metal before any MRI is considered.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 62-year-old smoker has a tongue-base SCC. On MRI, the imaging feature that most specifically upstages disease by indicating perineural spread is:
options: Bright T2 signal within the tumour
A 0.8 cm oval level II node with a fatty hilum
Enhancing tumour signal tracking along a nerve into a skull-base foramen with widening of that foramen
Restricted diffusion within the primary tumour
Fat stranding in the subcutaneous tissues
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: Enhancing tumour signal tracking along a nerve into a skull-base foramen with widening of that foramen
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Perineural spread is seen as abnormal enhancement and thickening of a nerve, often with foraminal widening and loss of the normal fat around the foramen. It upstages disease, worsens prognosis and changes radiotherapy planning. Bright T2 and restricted diffusion are non-specific; an 0.8 cm node with a fatty hilum is benign-appearing.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: Which single MRI nodal feature is the most specific for metastatic involvement in head & neck cancer?
options: Short-axis diameter greater than 1 cm
Homogeneous enhancement
Presence of a fatty hilum
Oval (reniform) shape
Central necrosis (non-enhancing core)
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: A necrotic (non-enhancing) centre is highly specific for nodal metastasis. Size alone is unreliable, a fatty hilum and oval shape suggest a benign node, and homogeneous enhancement is non-specific. Extranodal extension is the other strongly prognostic feature.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A patient with a bulky supraglottic tumour presents with stridor and increasing respiratory distress, and is booked for a staging MRI neck. The most appropriate immediate action is:
options: Proceed with the MRI to define the tumour before intervening
Secure the airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support before imaging
Give oral contrast and rescan
Arrange an outpatient PET-CT instead
Start high-dose IV gadolinium and steroids and continue to the scanner
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: Secure the airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support before imaging
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Stridor with respiratory distress signals critical airway obstruction — a supine MRI could precipitate complete obstruction. Airway is the priority: senior anaesthetic and ENT input for awake fibreoptic intubation or a surgical airway. Imaging follows once the airway is safe.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 46-year-old man of southern Chinese descent presents with a 6-week history of a painless left-sided neck lump and left-sided reduced hearing with a middle-ear effusion. Which single investigation best assesses the likely primary site and its local extent?
options: Plain lateral neck radiograph
Tympanometry alone
Pure-tone audiometry
MRI of the nasopharynx and neck with contrast
Ultrasound of the thyroid gland
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: MRI of the nasopharynx and neck with contrast
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: The combination of a cervical node and unilateral serous otitis media in an at-risk adult is highly suggestive of NPC. Contrast MRI is the primary modality for assessing the nasopharyngeal primary, depth of invasion, skull-base/perineural spread and nodal disease.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: Which anatomical site is the characteristic location of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
options: Fossa of Rosenmüller
Pyriform fossa
Vallecula
Torus tubarius apex only
Vocal cords
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: NPC characteristically arises in the fossa of Rosenmüller (the lateral pharyngeal recess of the nasopharynx). The pyriform fossa and vallecula are hypopharyngeal/laryngeal sites, not nasopharyngeal.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: On MRI, which finding most specifically indicates early skull-base invasion by NPC and demonstrates the advantage of MRI over CT?
options: Enlarged jugulodigastric node
Mucosal thickening of the maxillary sinus
Loss of normal high-signal fatty marrow in the clivus on T1
A retention cyst in the sphenoid sinus
Symmetrical adenoidal enlargement
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: Loss of normal high-signal fatty marrow in the clivus on T1
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Replacement of bright fatty marrow signal on T1-weighted images signals tumour infiltration of the skull base. MRI detects this marrow change earlier and more sensitively than CT, which relies on cortical bone destruction.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 45-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless lump at the angle of the jaw. MRI shows a well-defined, lobulated, homogeneously T2-bright lesion confined to the superficial lobe of the parotid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Warthin tumour
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Sjögren's syndrome
Pleomorphic adenoma
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: A well-defined, lobulated, strikingly T2-bright superficial parotid lesion in a middle-aged patient is the classic pleomorphic adenoma — the commonest parotid tumour. It is benign but excised due to risk of malignant transformation. Warthin tumour typically occurs in older male smokers and is often bilateral with lower T2 signal.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a parotid mass and ipsilateral facial weakness. Which single feature most strongly indicates malignancy?
options: Well-defined margins
Facial nerve palsy
High T2 signal
Location in the superficial lobe
Slow growth over years
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy with a parotid mass strongly suggests malignant infiltration of the nerve and mandates urgent referral. Well-defined margins, high T2 signal, superficial location and slow growth are more typical of benign disease; malignant features include ill-defined margins, low T2 signal, perineural spread and nodes.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: Which statement about MRI safety in salivary gland imaging is correct?
options: The main magnetic field is switched off between scans
Gadolinium is completely safe in severe renal failure
Metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies are irrelevant to screening
A cardiac pacemaker is generally a contraindication to MRI
Ferromagnetic objects pose no projectile risk near the scanner
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: A cardiac pacemaker is generally a contraindication to MRI
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Traditional cardiac pacemakers/ICDs are generally contraindications (though some are MR-conditional). The magnet is always on, so ferromagnetic objects are a projectile hazard and zoning is enforced. Metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies must be screened for, and gadolinium carries nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk in severe renal impairment.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 68-year-old diabetic man has 3 weeks of severe left otalgia, granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, and now a new left facial and tongue weakness. MRI shows loss of normal T1 marrow signal in the left petrous apex and clivus with avid enhancement of adjacent soft tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Skull-base osteomyelitis (malignant otitis externa)
Clival chordoma
Glomus jugulare paraganglioma
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma with perineural spread
Cavernous sinus meningioma
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: The classic picture — elderly diabetic, severe otalgia, canal granulation tissue, evolving lower cranial neuropathies, plus MRI marrow replacement and enhancement spreading from the ear — is skull-base osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas. It is a medical emergency needing urgent IV anti-pseudomonal therapy.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A patient with known maxillary sinus squamous cell carcinoma develops new right cheek numbness. Which MRI sequence and finding would best confirm perineural tumour spread along V2?
options: Non-contrast T2 showing a bright sinus
Diffusion-weighted imaging showing restricted diffusion in the globe
Fat-suppressed post-gadolinium T1 showing loss of foraminal fat with an enhancing, thickened nerve
Time-of-flight MR angiography of the internal carotid
Gradient-echo showing susceptibility artefact in the sinus
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: Fat-suppressed post-gadolinium T1 showing loss of foraminal fat with an enhancing, thickened nerve
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Perineural spread is best shown on fat-suppressed post-contrast T1: normal fat within the foramen (e.g. foramen rotundum for V2) is replaced, and the nerve becomes thickened and enhancing. This upstages the cancer and MRI detects it before CT shows bony change.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: MRI of a patient with pulsatile tinnitus shows a mass centred on the right jugular foramen with a 'salt-and-pepper' appearance from multiple flow voids. What is the most likely lesion?
options: Clival chordoma
Esthesioneuroblastoma
Pituitary macroadenoma
Chondrosarcoma
Glomus jugulare (paraganglioma)
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: A hypervascular jugular foramen mass with a 'salt-and-pepper' pattern (salt = subacute haemorrhage/slow flow bright foci, pepper = signal voids from high-flow vessels) is the classic MRI appearance of a glomus jugulare paraganglioma, often presenting with pulsatile tinnitus.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 28-year-old with jaw clicking has a TMJ MRI. On the closed-mouth oblique sagittal image the disc lies anterior to the condyle, but on the open-mouth image it returns to its normal position between the condyle and articular eminence. What is the diagnosis?
options: Normal TMJ
Anterior disc displacement with reduction
Anterior disc displacement without reduction
Septic arthritis of the TMJ
Condylar fracture
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: The disc is displaced when the mouth is closed but recaptures (reduces) onto the condyle on opening — the classic pattern associated with clicking. Because it reduces, mouth opening is usually preserved.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: Which single feature makes MRI superior to CT for assessing the TMJ?
options: Better depiction of condylar cortical bone
Lower cost and faster acquisition
Ability to use iodinated contrast
Direct visualisation of the articular disc
Superior detection of osteophytes
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: Direct visualisation of the articular disc
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: The fibrocartilaginous disc is the key structure in internal derangement and is not seen on X-ray or CT. MRI images it directly. CT is actually better for cortical bone detail such as osteophytes.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.question: A 45-year-old reports progressively worsening restricted mouth opening ("locking"). MRI shows the disc anteriorly displaced on the closed-mouth view and STILL anteriorly displaced on the open-mouth view. Which statement is correct?
options: This is disc displacement without reduction and typically causes limited opening
This is disc displacement with reduction and typically causes clicking
This finding is a normal variant needing no follow-up
A joint effusion excludes internal derangement
The condyle has translated normally onto the disc
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.answer: This is disc displacement without reduction and typically causes limited opening
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.explanation: Failure of the disc to recapture on opening is displacement WITHOUT reduction — a mechanical block ("closed lock") that limits mouth opening, in contrast to the clicking seen when a displaced disc reduces.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 64-year-old man with known prostate cancer presents with 2 weeks of worsening mid-back pain and now bilateral leg weakness with a T6 sensory level. What is the most appropriate imaging?
options: Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine
MRI of the thoracic spine only
Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours
CT of the thoracic spine
Bone scintigraphy
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: This is suspected metastatic spinal cord compression. Deposits are often multilevel and the clinical sensory level is unreliable, so the whole neuraxis must be screened urgently (within 24h), not just the symptomatic region. Dexamethasone and specialist referral accompany imaging.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: On a sagittal T1-weighted whole-spine MRI, a vertebral metastasis is typically seen as:
options: A bright (high-signal) lesion because tumour contains fat
No change, as T1 does not show marrow
A bright lesion only after fat suppression
A signal void identical to cortical bone
A dark (low-signal) lesion replacing normal bright fatty marrow
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: A dark (low-signal) lesion replacing normal bright fatty marrow
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Normal vertebral marrow is bright on T1 due to fat. Metastatic tumour replaces this fatty marrow, so deposits appear as focal areas of low (dark) signal against the bright background.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to MRI whole spine?
options: Estimated GFR of 55 mL/min
A non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker
A titanium hip replacement
Mild claustrophobia
Previous lumbar laminectomy
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: A non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: A non-MRI-conditional pacemaker/ICD is a classic contraindication because the magnetic field can disrupt the device. Titanium implants and prior surgery are generally safe; mild claustrophobia can be managed; and an eGFR of 55 permits gadolinium — the concern (NSF) arises with severe renal impairment.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 68-year-old man reports 8 months of increasingly clumsy hands and an unsteady gait. Examination shows brisk reflexes in all four limbs, bilateral upgoing plantars and a positive Hoffmann's sign. Which MRI finding best explains his presentation?
options: Foraminal narrowing compressing a single C6 nerve root with a normal cord
A bright T2 CSF collar preserved around a normal-calibre cord
Pannus at C1–C2 with an intact transverse ligament and no subluxation
Multilevel canal stenosis with cord compression and high T2 signal within the cord
Loss of vertebral body height with marrow oedema but no canal compromise
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Multilevel canal stenosis with cord compression and high T2 signal within the cord
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: The picture is degenerative cervical myelopathy: UMN signs below the level plus clumsy hands and gait disturbance. The MRI correlate is multilevel stenosis compressing the cord with intrinsic high T2 signal (myelomalacia). A single-root lesion would give dermatomal arm pain, not diffuse UMN signs.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a diving accident with tetraparesis. CT shows no fracture. Which statement about cervical MRI is correct?
options: MRI can demonstrate cord contusion/oedema and ligamentous injury not seen on CT
MRI is contraindicated because CT has already excluded significant injury
MRI cannot assess the spinal cord and is only useful for bony detail
A normal CT reliably excludes cord injury, so MRI adds nothing
MRI should be delayed to an outpatient appointment given the normal CT
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: MRI can demonstrate cord contusion/oedema and ligamentous injury not seen on CT
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Neurology out of keeping with a normal CT is a classic indication for urgent MRI. MRI shows intrinsic cord signal change (contusion/oedema, high T2) and ligamentous disruption that CT misses. Traumatic cord injury is an emergency requiring urgent imaging and spinal referral.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: An 80-year-old with known cervical spondylosis falls forwards and hyperextends the neck. She has weakness that is markedly worse in the arms than the legs. CT shows no fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cervical radiculopathy from a single foraminal disc
Complete cord transection
Central cord syndrome
Rheumatoid atlantoaxial subluxation
Guillain-Barré syndrome
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Central cord syndrome
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Central cord syndrome typically occurs in older patients with a spondylotic canal after a hyperextension injury, often without fracture. The central cord fibres serving the arms are preferentially affected, so weakness is worse in the upper than lower limbs, with central cord high T2 signal on MRI.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 68-year-old man with known prostate cancer develops 2 weeks of mid-thoracic back pain, then leg weakness, a sensory level at the umbilicus and urinary retention. What is the single most appropriate immediate investigation?
options: CT of the thoracic spine only
Plain radiographs of the whole spine
Bone scintigraphy (isotope bone scan)
Lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
Urgent MRI of the whole spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Urgent MRI of the whole spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: This is metastatic spinal cord compression. MRI is the investigation of choice and must cover the WHOLE spine because MSCC is frequently multi-level; imaging only the symptomatic level risks missing further deposits. CT and plain films underdetect epidural disease and cord signal change; a bone scan and LP would delay definitive treatment.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which MRI feature most reliably points to a MALIGNANT rather than an osteoporotic thoracic vertebral compression fracture?
options: Retropulsion of a posterior bony fragment
Complete replacement of the vertebral body marrow with pedicle involvement and a convex posterior cortex
A thin band of subchondral marrow oedema
Preserved normal fatty (T1-bright) marrow in adjacent vertebrae
Multiple old wedge deformities at other levels
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Complete replacement of the vertebral body marrow with pedicle involvement and a convex posterior cortex
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Malignant collapse shows complete T1 marrow replacement, pedicle (posterior element) involvement, a bulging/convex posterior cortex and often an epidural or paraspinal soft-tissue mass. Retropulsion of a fragment, band-like oedema, preserved fatty marrow and multiple old wedge deformities all favour a benign osteoporotic fracture.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 72-year-old man has 6 months of progressive leg weakness and a spastic gait. MRI shows diffuse high T2 signal and swelling of the lower thoracic cord with serpiginous flow voids along its dorsal surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic spinal cord compression
Idiopathic transverse myelitis
Thoracic disc herniation
Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula
Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Dorsal serpiginous flow voids with diffuse lower thoracic cord oedema in an elderly man are classic for a spinal dural AV fistula — a treatable but easily missed cause of progressive myelopathy. There is no vertebral marrow lesion or epidural mass (against MSCC/fracture), the signal change is not the discrete long central plaque of transverse myelitis, and there is no herniated disc compressing the cord.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 46-year-old presents with acute right-leg sciatica following lifting. MRI shows a right paracentral disc protrusion at the L5/S1 level. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
options: Right S1 root
Right L4 root
Right L5 root
Right S2 root
Bilateral cauda equina roots
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Right S1 root
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: A paracentral (posterolateral) disc compresses the traversing root, which at the L5/S1 level is the S1 root. This fits S1 features: lateral foot/sole sensory loss, weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle jerk. A far-lateral L5/S1 disc would instead catch the exiting L5 root.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 72-year-old describes bilateral aching leg pain and heaviness after walking 100 metres, eased by leaning forward on a shopping trolley or sitting. Foot pulses are palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Peripheral vascular (intermittent) claudication
Bilateral acute disc extrusion at L4/5
Neurogenic claudication from lumbar central canal stenosis
Cauda equina syndrome
Trochanteric bursitis
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar central canal stenosis
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Posture-dependent relief (flexion/sitting), the shopping-trolley sign and preserved pulses point to neurogenic claudication from central stenosis. Vascular claudication is relieved by stopping regardless of posture with absent pulses. There are no cauda equina red flags (no saddle anaesthesia, retention or reduced anal tone).

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 38-year-old with a week of low back and bilateral leg pain now reports difficulty passing urine, numbness when wiping, and new faecal incontinence. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and advise conservative management with analgesia for 6 weeks
Arrange routine outpatient lumbar MRI within 6 weeks
Request plain lumbar spine radiographs
Refer for outpatient physiotherapy
Arrange emergency same-day MRI of the whole lumbosacral spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Arrange emergency same-day MRI of the whole lumbosacral spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Bilateral sciatica with urinary dysfunction, saddle numbness and bowel incontinence is cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency. It requires immediate MRI of the whole lumbosacral spine and urgent decompression; any delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction. Conservative management, routine imaging or plain films are inappropriate.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 68-year-old man with known prostate cancer presents with 3 weeks of worsening thoracic back pain, now with bilateral leg weakness and difficulty passing urine. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
options: Plain radiograph of the thoracic spine
MRI of the whole spine
CT of the lumbar spine only
Bone scintigraphy (isotope bone scan)
Nerve conduction studies
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: MRI of the whole spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: This is metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours is the gold standard because it detects cord compression, defines cord signal change, and identifies multiple-level disease which is common and would be missed on a targeted scan.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which drug should be given immediately to a patient with confirmed or strongly suspected MSCC, alongside a proton pump inhibitor?
options: Intravenous ceftriaxone
Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin as treatment dose
Oral gabapentin
High-dose dexamethasone
Intravenous mannitol
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: High-dose dexamethasone
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: High-dose dexamethasone reduces peri-tumoural cord oedema and is started immediately while definitive treatment (surgery or radiotherapy) is arranged. A PPI is co-prescribed for gastric protection. It is given in parallel with, not after, imaging and referral.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which statement about MSCC best explains why treatment is time-critical?
options: Neurological function present at the time of treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome, and paraplegia rarely recovers
MRI signal change resolves within hours so scanning must be immediate
Dexamethasone loses efficacy if given more than 6 hours after symptom onset
Back pain is always the last symptom to appear
Radiotherapy can only be delivered within 24 hours of diagnosis
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Neurological function present at the time of treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome, and paraplegia rarely recovers
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Outcome tracks the patient's neurological status at treatment: an ambulant patient treated promptly usually stays mobile, whereas once a patient is paraplegic, recovery is rare. This is why whole-spine MRI and treatment are needed urgently, ideally within 24 hours.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A cancer patient is scheduled for urgent spinal MRI. Which finding on safety screening is the most important absolute contraindication to check for?
options: A titanium hip replacement inserted 5 years ago
Dental amalgam fillings
A non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker
A history of claustrophobia
Recent contrast-enhanced CT
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: A non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: An older/non-conditional pacemaker or ICD is a key MRI contraindication and must be screened for, along with cochlear implants, some aneurysm clips and metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies. Modern orthopaedic implants and dental amalgam are generally MRI-safe; claustrophobia is a practical issue, not an absolute contraindication.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which feature in the history most strongly suggests early MSCC and should prompt urgent MRI even before weakness develops?
options: Mechanical low back pain relieved by rest
Unilateral sciatica improving over 2 weeks
Chronic stable back pain of 10 years' duration
Localised muscular tenderness after heavy lifting
New progressive thoracic back pain that is worse at night and on coughing
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: New progressive thoracic back pain that is worse at night and on coughing
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Progressive, nocturnal back pain worsened by coughing or lying flat is the classic early red-flag symptom of MSCC and typically precedes weakness by weeks. In a cancer patient this warrants urgent whole-spine MRI before neurological deficit becomes established.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 42-year-old man presents with 12 hours of bilateral leg pain, numbness of the perineum, and reports his urinary stream "feels different" though he is still passing urine. Neurological exam shows reduced ankle reflexes. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
options: Plain lumbar spine radiographs
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Nerve conduction studies
CT lumbar spine without contrast
Outpatient MRI within 6 weeks
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: The picture — bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and altered urinary sensation with reduced reflexes — is cauda equina syndrome at the incomplete (CES-I) stage. MRI is the definitive test and must be done as an emergency, before progression to painless retention (CES-R) worsens prognosis. Plain films/CT and NCS would delay definitive imaging, and outpatient MRI is unacceptable.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: Which cause is most commonly responsible for cauda equina syndrome?
options: Metastatic tumour compressing the thecal sac
Epidural abscess
Traumatic burst fracture with retropulsion
Large central intervertebral disc herniation at L4/5 or L5/S1
Ankylosing spondylitis
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Large central intervertebral disc herniation at L4/5 or L5/S1
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: A large central disc prolapse at L4/5 or L5/S1 is the single commonest cause. Tumour, epidural abscess/haematoma, and trauma are important but less common differentials that the MRI also helps identify or exclude.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A patient with suspected cauda equina syndrome is confirmed on MRI to have a compressive central disc. Regarding definitive management, which statement is most accurate?
options: Urgent surgical decompression, ideally within 48 hours of onset
Treat conservatively with analgesia and review in clinic in 2 weeks
Start high-dose oral steroids and repeat MRI in 72 hours
Refer for elective physiotherapy and a lumbar corset
Await development of urinary retention before referring to surgery
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Urgent surgical decompression, ideally within 48 hours of onset
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Confirmed CES requires urgent surgical decompression, ideally within 48 hours of onset and sooner for incomplete CES, to preserve bladder, bowel and sexual function. Conservative measures, steroids alone, physiotherapy, or waiting for retention all risk permanent, irreversible deficit.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 54-year-old man who injects drugs presents with 3 weeks of worsening lower back pain and fever. MRI lumbar spine shows high T2/STIR signal in the L3/4 disc with marrow oedema (low T1, high STIR) in the L3 and L4 vertebral endplates, and post-gadolinium enhancement crossing the disc space. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic vertebral disease
Osteoporotic wedge fracture
Pyogenic spondylodiscitis
Schmorl's node
Degenerative Modic type II change
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Infection crossing the disc space with endplate marrow oedema in two adjacent vertebrae and enhancement is the hallmark of pyogenic spondylodiscitis. Malignancy typically spares the disc; the IVDU risk factor and fever further support infection (commonest organism S. aureus).

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A patient with known spondylodiscitis develops new bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention. Repeat MRI shows a posterior rim-enhancing epidural collection compressing the thecal sac and cord. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge on oral antibiotics and review in clinic
Await disc biopsy results before any intervention
Start physiotherapy and repeat MRI in 6 weeks
Reassure — epidural collections resolve spontaneously
Urgent surgical decompression/drainage plus IV antibiotics
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Urgent surgical decompression/drainage plus IV antibiotics
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: An epidural abscess causing cord compression with new neurology is a surgical emergency. Emergency decompression/drainage plus IV antibiotics is required; delaying for biopsy results or conservative management risks permanent neurological damage.

investigations__MRI__Spine.question: A 40-year-old presents with chronic back pain, weight loss and night sweats. MRI shows destruction of two contiguous vertebral bodies with relative preservation of the intervening disc, subligamentous spread, a paraspinal collection tracking into the psoas, and an angular kyphosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Staphylococcal pyogenic discitis
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease)
Multiple myeloma
Ankylosing spondylitis
Osteomyelitis from direct surgical contamination
investigations__MRI__Spine.answer: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease)
investigations__MRI__Spine.explanation: Vertebral body destruction with relative disc sparing, subligamentous multilevel spread, a psoas 'cold' abscess and gibbus (angular kyphosis) are characteristic of spinal TB. Pyogenic infection typically involves the disc early, and the systemic B-symptoms fit TB.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 24-year-old footballer twists his knee, feels a pop, and develops a rapid tense effusion. MRI shows discontinuous ACL fibres, anterior tibial translation, and marrow oedema at the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau. Which additional bony finding is most classically associated with this injury?
options: Osgood–Schlatter tibial tubercle fragmentation
Patellar sleeve avulsion
Segond fracture of the lateral tibial rim
Pellegrini–Stieda calcification of the MCL
Fabella os in the lateral gastrocnemius
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Segond fracture of the lateral tibial rim
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: A Segond fracture is a small avulsion off the lateral tibial rim that is highly associated with ACL rupture. Pellegrini–Stieda relates to chronic MCL injury; the others are unrelated to acute ACL tears.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A patient's knee is mechanically locked and cannot fully extend. Sagittal MRI shows a fragment lying in the intercondylar notch beneath the posterior cruciate ligament. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete PCL rupture
Cyclops lesion
Osteochondral loose body from the patella
Ganglion cyst of the ACL
Displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear (double PCL sign)
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear (double PCL sign)
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: A displaced longitudinal (bucket-handle) meniscal fragment flips into the notch under the PCL, producing the "double PCL sign" and a mechanically locked knee that warrants urgent orthopaedic referral.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: Which statement about imaging the acutely injured knee is correct?
options: MRI is the first-line test for every acute knee injury
The Ottawa knee rules help decide who needs an X-ray to exclude fracture
X-ray reliably demonstrates meniscal and cruciate ligament tears
MRI uses ionising radiation, so it should be avoided in young patients
A normal X-ray excludes internal derangement of the knee
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: The Ottawa knee rules help decide who needs an X-ray to exclude fracture
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Acute knees are assessed clinically first, with the Ottawa knee rules guiding X-ray for fracture. X-ray cannot show menisci or ligaments; MRI (no ionising radiation) is reserved for suspected soft-tissue injury or surgical planning.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 58-year-old presents with chronic shoulder pain and weakness. MRI shows a fluid-signal gap traversing the full thickness of the supraspinatus tendon, retraction of the tendon to the level of the glenoid, and fatty infiltration of the supraspinatus muscle belly. Which feature most strongly indicates the tear is chronic and likely irreparable?
options: The location in the supraspinatus tendon
Presence of a fluid-signal gap
Subacromial bursal fluid
Fatty infiltration of the muscle belly
Increased signal in the tendon
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Fatty infiltration of the muscle belly
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Muscle atrophy with fatty infiltration (Goutallier grade) does not reverse after surgical repair and is the key marker of a chronic, irreparable tear and poor surgical outcome. A fluid gap and tendon signal indicate a tear but not chronicity/reparability.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 22-year-old rugby player sustained an anterior shoulder dislocation. Which combination of MRI findings would you most expect?
options: Anteroinferior labral (Bankart) tear with a posterosuperolateral humeral head impaction (Hill–Sachs)
Superior labral tear with a biceps anchor lesion
Thickened coracohumeral ligament and axillary recess oedema
Low-signal calcific deposit within the supraspinatus tendon
Subscapularis tear with medial biceps dislocation
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Anteroinferior labral (Bankart) tear with a posterosuperolateral humeral head impaction (Hill–Sachs)
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Anterior dislocation classically produces a Bankart lesion (anteroinferior labrum) and its paired Hill–Sachs impaction fracture on the posterosuperolateral humeral head. The other options describe SLAP, adhesive capsulitis, calcific tendinitis and biceps/subscapularis pathology respectively.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: Which statement about shoulder MRI and its use is correct?
options: Most shoulder pain requires MRI as the first-line investigation
Calcific tendinitis appears as high signal on all MRI sequences
MR arthrography with intra-articular gadolinium is the best test for labral tears
The MRI magnet can be switched off between patients to allow safe entry
Adhesive capsulitis shows a fluid-signal tendon gap
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: MR arthrography with intra-articular gadolinium is the best test for labral tears
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Intra-articular gadolinium distends the joint and tracks into labral tears, making MR arthrography the gold standard. Most shoulder pain is managed conservatively without MRI; calcific deposits are low signal on all sequences; the magnet is always on; and adhesive capsulitis shows capsular thickening/oedema, not a tendon gap.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: An 82-year-old woman is unable to weight-bear after a fall and has left hip pain with a shortened, externally rotated leg on exertion. AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy
Repeat plain radiographs in two weeks
Bone densitometry (DEXA) scan
Diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection
MRI of the hip/pelvis to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: MRI of the hip/pelvis to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Around 10% of femoral neck fractures are occult on initial X-ray. In an elderly patient who cannot weight-bear, MRI is the gold standard and reveals a fracture line with marrow oedema. Discharging or waiting risks displacement; CT is the alternative if MRI is unavailable.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 34-year-old man on long-term high-dose corticosteroids develops progressive right groin pain. Radiographs are normal. MRI shows an anterosuperior subchondral lesion in the femoral head with an inner bright and outer dark band on T2. What is the diagnosis?
options: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Acetabular labral tear
Femoral neck stress fracture
Osteoid osteoma
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: The "double-line sign" (inner bright granulation tissue, outer dark sclerosis) in an anterosuperior subchondral location on a patient with steroid exposure is characteristic of AVN. MRI detects it pre-collapse, before X-ray changes, allowing joint-preserving options.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 21-year-old long-distance runner has 3 weeks of worsening groin pain, worse on impact, with normal radiographs. MRI shows marrow oedema of the femoral neck with a faint line on its superolateral aspect. What is the key concern that guides management?
options: It is a benign enthesopathy needing no follow-up
It represents referred pain from the lumbar spine
It is diagnostic of septic arthritis of the hip
The tension-side location risks progression to a displaced fracture
It confirms transient osteoporosis and will resolve spontaneously
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: The tension-side location risks progression to a displaced fracture
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: A femoral neck stress fracture on the superolateral (tension) side is unstable and can displace, so it warrants urgent offloading/non-weight-bearing and orthopaedic referral. MRI detects these before radiographic change; compression-side fractures are lower risk but still need monitoring.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes has a chronic ulcer over the plantar forefoot. MRI shows the underlying metatarsal head with low T1 marrow signal, high STIR signal, avid enhancement, and a sinus tract extending from the ulcer to the cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteomyelitis
Charcot neuroarthropathy
Bone stress injury (march fracture)
Osteochondral lesion
Simple soft-tissue cellulitis only
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: T1 marrow REPLACEMENT with high STIR signal, enhancement, and — crucially — a sinus tract from an adjacent ulcer to the bone is diagnostic of contiguous osteomyelitis. Charcot is joint-centred in the midfoot without an ulcer/sinus tract; a stress fracture shows a fracture line without a sinus tract.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 40-year-old sprinter has sudden calf pain and cannot push off. MRI shows complete discontinuity of the Achilles fibres with a fluid-filled gap and retracted tendon ends. Which clinical finding fits this MRI appearance?
options: Positive anterior drawer of the ankle
Tenderness over the tarsal navicular
Positive Simmonds/Thompson test (no plantarflexion on calf squeeze)
Palpable intermetatarsal mass
Thickened plantar fascia on palpation
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Positive Simmonds/Thompson test (no plantarflexion on calf squeeze)
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Fibre discontinuity with a gap indicates full-thickness Achilles rupture, which clinically gives a positive Simmonds/Thompson (calf squeeze) test with absent plantarflexion. Anterior drawer tests lateral ligaments; the other options relate to different pathologies.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A diabetic patient presents with a swollen, deformed midfoot. MRI shows tarsometatarsal fragmentation, subluxation, subchondral cysts and a rocker-bottom deformity, joint-centred oedema, and NO overlying ulcer or sinus tract. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteomyelitis
Morton's neuroma
Talar dome osteochondral lesion
Necrotising fasciitis
Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Midfoot (tarsometatarsal/Lisfranc) fragmentation with deformity, joint-centred changes, rocker-bottom foot and an intact skin envelope (no ulcer/sinus tract) are classic for Charcot arthropathy. The absence of a skin breach and the joint-centred, midfoot distribution argue against contiguous osteomyelitis.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 24-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial loading of the thumb. Wrist X-rays including scaphoid views are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with reassurance and simple analgesia
Immobilise in a below-elbow cast and arrange MRI of the wrist
Repeat the identical X-ray series the same day
Refer for immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Arrange nerve conduction studies
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Immobilise in a below-elbow cast and arrange MRI of the wrist
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray is a clinically suspected occult scaphoid fracture. The wrist must be immobilised and re-imaged with MRI, the gold-standard test. Discharging risks a missed fracture, AVN and non-union.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: Why is a fracture of the scaphoid waist particularly at risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole?
options: The scaphoid has no periosteal covering
The proximal pole is composed only of cartilage
The radial artery is routinely damaged in all FOOSH injuries
The scaphoid's blood supply is retrograde, entering distally, so a waist fracture devascularises the proximal fragment
The lunate compresses the scaphoid vessels after fracture
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: The scaphoid's blood supply is retrograde, entering distally, so a waist fracture devascularises the proximal fragment
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the scaphoid distally and perfuses it retrogradely towards the proximal pole. A waist or proximal-pole fracture cuts off this supply, causing proximal-pole AVN and non-union.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 30-year-old presents with chronic ulnar-sided wrist pain and clicking, worse on gripping and ulnar deviation, with normal X-rays. Which structure is MRI most likely to show as injured?
options: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)
Scapholunate ligament
Lunate (Kienbock's disease)
Median nerve within the carpal tunnel
Extensor pollicis longus tendon
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Ulnar-sided wrist pain with clicking, worse on gripping and ulnar deviation, is the classic presentation of a TFCC tear. MRI (or MR arthrography) demonstrates the tear as high fluid signal disrupting the normally low-signal fibrocartilage.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 45-year-old builder develops lateral elbow pain worse on gripping and resisted wrist extension. MRI shows thickening and increased T2 signal at the origin of the common extensor tendon. Which specific tendon is most characteristically involved?
options: Extensor carpi ulnaris
Pronator teres
Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
Flexor carpi radialis
Brachioradialis
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) predominantly involves the ECRB component of the common extensor origin. The flexor–pronator group (pronator teres, FCR) is affected in medial epicondylitis.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 20-year-old baseball pitcher has medial elbow pain and valgus laxity. Which imaging investigation is most sensitive for a suspected partial ulnar collateral ligament tear?
options: Plain radiograph
Ultrasound of the flexor origin
CT without contrast
Nerve conduction studies
MR arthrography of the elbow
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: MR arthrography is most sensitive for UCL injury; intra-articular contrast tracking beneath a partially detached distal anterior bundle produces the classic "T sign". The UCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress in throwers.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.question: A 50-year-old man felt a sudden painful pop lifting a heavy box; he now has weak supination, a retracted "reverse Popeye" bulge and a palpable antecubital gap. What is the single most important MRI determination guiding management?
options: Presence of an elbow joint effusion
Whether the rupture is complete or partial
Signal in the ulnar nerve
Status of the radial head cortex
Presence of a posterior fat-pad sign
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.answer: Whether the rupture is complete or partial
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.explanation: Distal biceps rupture is a surgical red flag. MRI (FABS view) defines complete vs partial rupture and degree of retraction, which decides whether prompt anatomical repair is needed before the tendon retracts and scars.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 26-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and has anatomical snuffbox tenderness. Initial wrist X-ray is normal. MRI performed shows, at the scaphoid waist, a linear focus that is dark on all sequences with surrounding tissue that is low on T1 and high on STIR. What does the STIR-bright, T1-low tissue represent?
options: Sclerosis around a healed old fracture
Normal fatty marrow
Marrow oedema around an acute occult fracture
Avascular necrosis with double-line sign
Enchondroma
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Marrow oedema around an acute occult fracture
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: An X-ray-occult scaphoid fracture shows a fracture line dark on all sequences with surrounding marrow oedema (low T1, high STIR). MRI reveals this before radiographic change, which is why it is used for clinically suspected but radiographically normal scaphoid injuries. Sclerosis would be low on T2/STIR, and normal fatty marrow is bright on T1.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 45-year-old on long-term high-dose corticosteroids has hip pain. X-ray is normal. Hip MRI shows a subchondral serpentine lesion in the femoral head with, on T2, an inner bright line and an outer dark line. What is the diagnosis?
options: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
Septic arthritis
Femoral neck stress fracture
Metastatic deposit
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: The double-line sign (inner bright granulation tissue, outer dark sclerosis) in a subchondral femoral head lesion is characteristic of avascular necrosis. Steroids are a classic risk factor, and MRI detects AVN pre-collapse before X-ray change. Transient osteoporosis shows diffuse oedema without a demarcated necrotic segment or double-line sign.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 70-year-old with back pain has a sagittal T1 spine sequence showing diffuse marrow signal that is darker than the intervertebral discs, with several focal lesions. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: This is normal fatty marrow and needs no action
Diffuse low-T1 marrow darker than disc suggests malignant infiltration and warrants investigation
Marrow brighter than disc on T1 always indicates malignancy
STIR is unnecessary for assessing myeloma
AVN is the most likely diagnosis
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Diffuse low-T1 marrow darker than disc suggests malignant infiltration and warrants investigation
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: Normal adult marrow is brighter than muscle and disc on T1. Marrow that is darker than the disc indicates fat replacement — in a diffuse pattern with focal lesions this suggests metastatic or myelomatous infiltration and mandates investigation, with attention to pathological fracture risk. Whole-body STIR is standard for myeloma, and the double-line sign (not this pattern) indicates AVN.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 7-year-old presents with a 5-day history of fever and refusal to bear weight on the left leg. X-ray of the tibia is normal. MRI is arranged. Which MRI finding would be MOST specific for acute osteomyelitis?
options: Reticulated high signal in the subcutaneous fat
A joint effusion with synovial enhancement
Thickened enhancing tendon sheaths
Confluent low-signal marrow on T1 replacing normal fatty marrow, with high STIR and enhancement
A small non-enhancing collection in the adjacent muscle
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Confluent low-signal marrow on T1 replacing normal fatty marrow, with high STIR and enhancement
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: Osteomyelitis is a marrow disease. Confluent T1 marrow replacement (loss of the normal bright fatty signal) with high T2/STIR and enhancement is the most specific sign. Reticulated subcutaneous signal indicates cellulitis, an effusion with synovial enhancement suggests septic arthritis, and an intramuscular collection is an abscess/pyomyositis — none are specific to bone infection. In children, haematogenous osteomyelitis classically involves the metaphysis of long bones, most often due to Staph aureus.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has a rapidly spreading, dusky lower-limb erythema. Pain is far worse than the skin appearance suggests, he is hypotensive and pyrexial, and there is palpable crepitus. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Immediate surgical debridement with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Urgent MRI with gadolinium before any intervention
Outpatient oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
CT with contrast to look for fascial gas, then decide
Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the subcutaneous tissue
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Immediate surgical debridement with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: This is necrotising fasciitis — pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and crepitus. It is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency; survival depends on immediate debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics. Imaging (MRI or CT) may show fluid and gas tracking along deep fascia but must NEVER delay theatre. Oral antibiotics and outpatient review would be fatal.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 45-year-old diabetic has a plantar forefoot ulcer that probes to bone. MRI shows marrow oedema in the adjacent metatarsal head with an overlying enhancing sinus tract and cortical erosion. Which statement best fits this picture?
options: This is Charcot neuro-arthropathy, typically centred on the midfoot with no skin ulcer
The findings are diagnostic of a bone bruise from pressure
This is osteomyelitis by contiguous spread from the ulcer
Marrow oedema beneath an ulcer excludes infection
This appearance mandates immediate MRI-guided joint aspiration
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: This is osteomyelitis by contiguous spread from the ulcer
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: Marrow oedema at a pressure point directly beneath an ulcer that probes to bone, with a sinus tract and cortical erosion, indicates osteomyelitis from contiguous spread — the dominant route in the diabetic foot. Charcot arthropathy is instead centred on joints (classically the Lisfranc/midfoot), causes deformity, and characteristically has NO overlying ulcer or sinus. The presence of a sinus tract and cortical breach strongly favours infection over a purely neuropathic process.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A 58-year-old man has a firm, painless 7 cm lump deep in the thigh that has grown over 3 months. What is the single most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and review in 6 months
Arrange local excision under GA to obtain a diagnosis
Ultrasound-guided aspiration in the GP surgery
Start empirical antibiotics for a presumed abscess
Urgent referral to a sarcoma unit with MRI of the primary and CT chest
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Urgent referral to a sarcoma unit with MRI of the primary and CT chest
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: A deep, enlarging lump >5 cm meets sarcoma red-flag (2-week-wait) criteria. It must be referred, imaged with MRI (local staging) and CT chest (lung metastases), and biopsied — NOT excised blindly, which risks a tumour-seeding "whoops" resection.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: Which statement about MRI in the assessment of a soft-tissue mass is correct?
options: MRI reliably distinguishes benign from malignant lesions on signal alone, so biopsy is unnecessary
MRI defines size, compartment and relationship to the neurovascular bundle for surgical planning
CT is superior to MRI for soft-tissue contrast in the limbs
MRI is contraindicated in all soft-tissue masses
A high-signal lesion on T2 always indicates a benign cyst
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: MRI defines size, compartment and relationship to the neurovascular bundle for surgical planning
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: MRI's strength is local characterisation and staging — size, compartment, and neurovascular/bone relationships. It cannot reliably separate benign from malignant on signal alone, so image-guided core biopsy remains essential. Myxoid tumours can mimic cysts on T2 but enhance.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A digital soft-tissue lesion shows marked low signal with "blooming" artefact on gradient-echo (GRE) MRI sequences. What is the most likely underlying cause of this appearance?
options: Fat within the lesion
Simple fluid
Calcified phleboliths
Haemosiderin deposition
Gadolinium enhancement
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: Blooming on GRE is caused by the magnetic susceptibility of haemosiderin. This is characteristic of giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath / pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS), which contain haemosiderin from recurrent microhaemorrhage.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.question: A patient has a 7 cm firm mass deep to the fascia in the thigh that is enlarging. What is the correct next step?
options: Refer to a sarcoma unit for MRI + planned core biopsy
Excise (shell out) the lump in clinic
Reassure — deep lumps are usually lipomas
Aspirate for cytology
Start antibiotics for an abscess
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.answer: Refer to a sarcoma unit for MRI + planned core biopsy
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.explanation: A deep (subfascial), >5 cm, growing soft-tissue mass is a sarcoma until proven otherwise. It must be referred to a sarcoma unit for MRI and image-guided core biopsy along a planned excision track — an unplanned local excision ("whoops procedure") compromises limb-salvage surgery.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 58-year-old woman on trastuzumab for breast cancer needs accurate serial monitoring of her left ventricular ejection fraction. Which modality is the gold standard for this reproducible measurement?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography
Gated SPECT myocardial perfusion
Cardiac MRI
Coronary CT angiography
Chest radiography
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: CMR is the gold standard for ventricular volumes and EF because it is highly reproducible, making it ideal for serial monitoring of chemotherapy (e.g. trastuzumab) cardiotoxicity. Echo is more operator-dependent and relies on geometric assumptions.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: By what method does cardiac MRI derive left ventricular volumes from a short-axis cine stack?
options: A single-plane length x diameter geometric formula
Doppler velocity-time integral across the outflow tract
Thermodilution across the pulmonary artery
Planimetry of a single mid-ventricular slice
Summation of contiguous slice volumes (Simpson's method of discs)
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Summation of contiguous slice volumes (Simpson's method of discs)
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: CMR traces contours on each contiguous short-axis slice and sums slice area x thickness (Simpson's method), so volumes require no geometric assumptions — a key advantage over echo.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: Which of the following is the most important safety check before performing a cardiac MRI?
options: Serum potassium level
Presence and MR-conditional status of any implanted cardiac device
Recent iodinated contrast administration
Fasting status for the preceding 6 hours
Ambient room temperature
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Presence and MR-conditional status of any implanted cardiac device
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Non-conditional pacemakers/ICDs are historically a contraindication to MRI; many modern devices are MR-conditional, so the device must always be checked. Iodinated contrast is not used in CMR (gadolinium is, with caution in renal impairment).

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A patient with ischaemic cardiomyopathy has a hypokinetic anterior wall. LGE shows enhancement involving <25% of the wall thickness in that segment. What does this predict?
options: The segment is dense scar and will not recover
The pattern indicates a non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy
Gadolinium is contraindicated in this patient
Function is likely to recover after revascularisation (viable/hibernating myocardium)
The segment shows no viable myocardium
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Function is likely to recover after revascularisation (viable/hibernating myocardium)
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Less than 25% transmural scar indicates predominantly viable, hibernating myocardium; restoring perfusion by revascularisation should improve contractile function. >50% transmurality predicts non-recovery.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: An LGE study shows a mid-wall linear stripe of enhancement not confined to any coronary territory and sparing the subendocardium. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: A non-ischaemic process such as dilated cardiomyopathy
Acute subendocardial infarction
Full-thickness transmural infarct
Normal nulling of myocardium
Coronary artery occlusion of the LAD
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: A non-ischaemic process such as dilated cardiomyopathy
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Ischaemic scar begins subendocardially and follows a coronary territory. Mid-wall or epicardial enhancement sparing the subendocardium in a non-coronary distribution indicates non-ischaemic disease (cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, infiltration).

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: On a standard LGE inversion-recovery image, why does normal myocardium appear black while scar appears bright?
options: Scar contains no gadolinium so it is nulled to black
Normal muscle retains gadolinium longest
The inversion time is chosen to null normal myocardium, and retained gadolinium in scar makes it bright
Bright tissue represents fat, not scar
The sequence images gadolinium immediately after injection before any washout
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: The inversion time is chosen to null normal myocardium, and retained gadolinium in scar makes it bright
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: The inversion recovery TI is set so signal from normal myocardium is nulled (black). Scar retains extracellular gadolinium with delayed washout, giving high signal (bright white). Imaging is performed ~10 min after injection.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 34-year-old man is investigated for exertional dyspnoea. Cardiac MRI shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 18 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and patchy mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement concentrated at the right ventricular insertion points. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Left ventricular non-compaction
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy ≥15 mm, LVOT obstruction with SAM, and patchy mid-wall LGE at the RV insertion points are the hallmark CMR features of HCM. The LGE distribution here also indicates the extent of fibrosis relevant to sudden-death risk.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 58-year-old woman has a dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Cardiac MRI shows a linear mid-wall stripe of late gadolinium enhancement in the septum, with no subendocardial involvement. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The LGE pattern indicates prior myocardial infarction
The mid-wall LGE indicates fibrosis and a worse prognosis in dilated cardiomyopathy
The absence of LGE excludes any cardiomyopathy
The pattern is diagnostic of ARVC
Gadolinium should be avoided because it cannot characterise fibrosis
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: The mid-wall LGE indicates fibrosis and a worse prognosis in dilated cardiomyopathy
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: A mid-wall septal stripe of LGE that spares the subendocardium is the non-ischaemic pattern seen in DCM; it marks fibrosis and worse prognosis. Infarction would give subendocardial/transmural LGE in a coronary territory, which is absent here.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 26-year-old presents with palpitations and a family history of sudden death. Cardiac MRI shows a dilated, poorly functioning right ventricle with regional wall-motion abnormalities, a free-wall aneurysm, and fibrofatty replacement. Which single statement is correct?
options: The findings are diagnostic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
MRI has no role in this condition and should not be performed
The findings indicate ischaemic cardiomyopathy
These findings contribute to the Task Force Criteria for ARVC
The findings mandate immediate cardiac transplantation
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: These findings contribute to the Task Force Criteria for ARVC
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: RV dilatation/dysfunction, regional wall-motion abnormalities, aneurysms and fibrofatty replacement are characteristic of ARVC and form part of the revised Task Force Criteria. CMR is central to diagnosis and to identifying features that inform ICD referral for sudden-death prevention.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 24-year-old man presents with chest pain and a raised troponin one week after a coryzal illness. Coronary angiography is normal. Cardiac MRI shows patchy subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement in the inferolateral wall with high T2 signal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute myocarditis
Acute myocardial infarction
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Cardiac sarcoidosis
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Raised troponin with unobstructed coronaries (MINOCA) plus CMR showing T2 oedema and subepicardial/mid-wall non-coronary LGE (inferolateral) meets the Lake Louise Criteria for myocarditis. A subepicardial distribution and preserved subendocardium argue against infarction.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: On cardiac MRI, which pattern of late gadolinium enhancement most reliably distinguishes acute myocardial infarction from myocarditis?
options: Subepicardial LGE in the inferolateral wall
Mid-wall LGE not confined to a coronary territory
Subendocardial or transmural LGE within a single coronary territory
Absence of any LGE
Diffuse global subepicardial LGE
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Subendocardial or transmural LGE within a single coronary territory
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Ischaemic injury begins in the subendocardium (most vulnerable to ischaemia) and follows a coronary vascular territory, giving subendocardial-to-transmural LGE. Myocarditis produces subepicardial/mid-wall LGE that does not respect coronary territories.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: Which of the following is the correct pairing of Lake Louise Criteria pillars used to diagnose myocarditis on CMR?
options: Subendocardial LGE and reduced ejection fraction
Pericardial effusion and elevated troponin
First-pass perfusion defect and coronary stenosis
Wall thinning and left atrial enlargement
Myocardial oedema on T2 imaging and non-ischaemic LGE with raised T1/ECV
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Myocardial oedema on T2 imaging and non-ischaemic LGE with raised T1/ECV
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: The updated Lake Louise Criteria require a T2-based marker of oedema plus a T1-based marker of non-ischaemic injury (subepicardial/mid-wall LGE, raised native T1 and ECV). The other options describe ischaemic or non-specific findings.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A patient with confirmed myocarditis develops hypotension, worsening breathlessness and complete heart block. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Reassure and discharge with exercise advice
Urgent cardiology/ICU referral and consideration of mechanical circulatory support
Start high-intensity exercise rehabilitation
Prescribe oral beta-blocker and review in clinic in 6 weeks
Repeat coronary angiography electively
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Urgent cardiology/ICU referral and consideration of mechanical circulatory support
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Haemodynamic instability, arrhythmia or heart block signals fulminant myocarditis, which is life-threatening and requires urgent cardiology/ICU input and possible mechanical support. Giant cell myocarditis should be considered given its aggressive course.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and thickened ventricular walls undergoes cardiac MRI. The radiographer reports difficulty nulling the myocardium on the TI scout, and images show diffuse global subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement with a very high extracellular volume. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cardiac sarcoidosis
Fabry disease
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Cardiac amyloidosis
Prior myocardial infarction
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: The combination of biventricular thickening, difficulty nulling the myocardium on the TI scout (abnormal gadolinium kinetics), diffuse GLOBAL SUBENDOCARDIAL LGE, and very high ECV is the hallmark of cardiac amyloidosis. Sarcoid gives patchy mid-wall/epicardial LGE, Fabry gives low native T1, and infarction follows a subendocardial coronary territory rather than a global non-coronary pattern.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with unexplained complete heart block. Cardiac MRI shows patchy mid-wall and epicardial late gadolinium enhancement concentrated in the basal septum. Which additional investigation best assesses disease activity to guide treatment?
options: FDG PET imaging
DPD/PYP bone scintigraphy
T2* mapping
Serum free light chains
Coronary angiography
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Basal septal patchy mid-wall/epicardial LGE with high-grade AV block in a young patient strongly suggests cardiac sarcoidosis. FDG PET detects active inflammation and guides immunosuppression, complementing CMR which shows established scar. Bone scintigraphy and light chains work up amyloid, T2* assesses iron, and angiography assesses coronary disease — none of which addresses sarcoid activity.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A transfusion-dependent thalassaemia patient is monitored with cardiac MRI. Which parameter is used to quantify myocardial iron, and how is it interpreted?
options: T2* mapping — a high value indicates high iron
Native T1 mapping — a high value indicates high iron
T2* mapping — a low value indicates high iron
Late gadolinium enhancement volume — proportional to iron
ECV — a low value indicates high iron
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: T2* mapping — a low value indicates high iron
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Iron shortens T2*, so LOW myocardial T2* signifies HIGH iron loading (T2* <20 ms abnormal, <10 ms high risk of heart failure/arrhythmia). This guides chelation therapy. LGE and ECV are not the primary tools for iron quantification, and iron overload characteristically lowers rather than raises native T1.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A 19-year-old with repaired Tetralogy of Fallot attends ACHD follow-up. Which single feature makes cardiac MRI the modality of choice for his lifelong surveillance?
options: It is cheaper and faster than transthoracic echocardiography
It is the only modality that can detect an atrial septal defect
It does not require any patient screening or preparation
It replaces the need for echocardiography in children
It provides radiation-free, reproducible right ventricular volume and function assessment
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: It provides radiation-free, reproducible right ventricular volume and function assessment
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: The defining advantage of CMR in CHD is accurate, reproducible RV volumetry and function with no ionising radiation — essential for repeated lifelong monitoring of RV dilatation from pulmonary regurgitation. It complements rather than replaces echo, and still requires safety screening.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: Phase-contrast CMR in a patient with an atrial septal defect shows pulmonary flow (Qp) of 9 L/min and systemic flow (Qs) of 4.5 L/min. Which statement is correct?
options: Qp:Qs is 1:1, indicating no shunt
Qp:Qs is 2:1, indicating a haemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt
This indicates a right-to-left shunt requiring urgent oxygen
The ratio cannot be calculated from phase-contrast data
A ratio this high excludes any need for defect closure
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Qp:Qs is 2:1, indicating a haemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: Qp:Qs = 9/4.5 = 2:1. A ratio of 1.5:1 or greater is a haemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt and generally warrants closure. Phase-contrast flow mapping across the pulmonary trunk and aorta is exactly how CMR derives these values.

investigations__MRI__Cardiac.question: A young adult with a large uncorrected VSD is now cyanosed with clubbing; CMR flow shows the shunt has become predominantly right-to-left. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
options: Coarctation of the aorta — measure the collateral flow
A normal variant — reassure and discharge
Contrast reaction to gadolinium — stop the scan
Eisenmenger syndrome from pulmonary hypertension — specialist ACHD referral, avoid routine closure
Anomalous pulmonary venous drainage — plan immediate surgery
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.answer: Eisenmenger syndrome from pulmonary hypertension — specialist ACHD referral, avoid routine closure
investigations__MRI__Cardiac.explanation: A long-standing significant left-to-right shunt can raise pulmonary vascular resistance until the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome), producing cyanosis and clubbing. This is a red flag needing specialist ACHD assessment; simple defect closure is contraindicated once irreversible pulmonary hypertension has developed.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 58-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain, a raised ALP and bilirubin, and ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct but no stone is seen. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Diagnostic ERCP to visualise the duct
CT abdomen with contrast
MRCP
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
Repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: With biochemical and sonographic evidence of biliary obstruction but no stone identified, MRCP is the non-invasive test of choice to look for choledocholithiasis or a stricture. It avoids the pancreatitis/perforation risks of ERCP and determines who genuinely needs a therapeutic ERCP.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: Why is a heavily T2-weighted sequence used in MRCP?
options: It makes flowing blood appear bright
It requires intravenous gadolinium to opacify the ducts
It uses ionising radiation to enhance duct contrast
It highlights calcified gallstones as bright signal
It makes static fluid such as bile and pancreatic juice appear very bright against dark soft tissue
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: It makes static fluid such as bile and pancreatic juice appear very bright against dark soft tissue
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Static/slow fluid has a long T2, so on heavily T2-weighted images bile and pancreatic juice stay very bright while background tissue and flowing blood appear dark. No contrast or radiation is used; stones appear as dark filling defects within the bright duct.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 70-year-old man with fever, RUQ pain and jaundice becomes hypotensive and confused. He has a stone obstructing the CBD. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent MRCP before any intervention
IV antibiotics, resuscitation and urgent ERCP for biliary drainage
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid and discharge
Await spontaneous stone passage with analgesia
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: IV antibiotics, resuscitation and urgent ERCP for biliary drainage
