investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: This is ascending cholangitis with Reynolds pentad (Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion) — a surgical emergency. The obstructed, infected biliary system must be decompressed urgently with therapeutic ERCP alongside antibiotics and resuscitation; diagnostic MRCP should not delay drainage.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 45-year-old woman has an incidental 4 cm liver lesion. MRI shows it is markedly hyperintense on T2 ("light bulb" bright) with peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement that fills in towards the centre on delayed images. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatic adenoma
Cholangiocarcinoma
Haemangioma
Colorectal metastasis
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Very bright T2 signal plus peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in is the classic signature of a haemangioma, the commonest benign liver lesion. HCC shows washout, adenoma does not typically fill in this way, and mets are usually multiple and hypovascular.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 60-year-old man with known cirrhosis has a new 3 cm nodule on surveillance MRI: arterial hyperenhancement, washout on the portal-venous phase, and an enhancing capsule. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose HCC on imaging and refer to the HCC MDT
Reassure and rescan in 12 months
Percutaneous biopsy is mandatory before any treatment
Treat as a simple cyst, no follow-up
Start empirical antibiotics for a suspected abscess
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Diagnose HCC on imaging and refer to the HCC MDT
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: In an at-risk cirrhotic liver, arterial hyperenhancement with washout and a capsule is the LI-RADS diagnostic signature of HCC, which can be diagnosed on imaging alone without biopsy. The correct action is MDT referral for staging and treatment planning.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 32-year-old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill has a solid liver lesion that enhances in the arterial phase but does NOT retain hepatobiliary contrast agent on the delayed hepatobiliary phase. Which lesion, and why does the distinction matter clinically?
options: Focal nodular hyperplasia — it is entirely benign and needs no action
Simple cyst — no malignant potential
Hepatic adenoma — risk of bleeding and malignant transformation
Haemangioma — light-bulb bright on T2
Metastasis — search for a primary tumour
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Hepatic adenoma — risk of bleeding and malignant transformation
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Failure to retain hepatobiliary contrast (unlike FNH, which does retain it and shows a central scar) points to a hepatic adenoma. Adenomas are associated with oestrogen/OCP and steroid use and carry a risk of haemorrhage and malignant change, so they may warrant OCP cessation and possible resection.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 45-year-old with metabolic syndrome has an MRI liver. On out-of-phase images the liver loses signal diffusely compared with in-phase images, with dark etching at organ margins. What does this indicate?
options: Diffuse hepatic iron overload
Hepatic fibrosis
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Normal liver
Diffuse hepatic steatosis (fat)
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Signal loss on OUT-of-phase images (with India-ink etching) is the chemical-shift signature of fat. Iron, by contrast, loses signal on IN-phase (longer-TE) images. The metabolic syndrome context fits NAFLD/MASLD.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A patient with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia is monitored for iron overload. Which MRI technique best quantifies liver iron concentration?
options: Proton density fat fraction (PDFF)
T2*/R2* mapping
MR elastography (MRE)
Diffusion-weighted imaging
Out-of-phase chemical shift imaging
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Iron shortens T2*; R2* (=1/T2*) is calibrated to liver iron concentration (LIC), guiding chelation. PDFF quantifies fat, MRE quantifies fibrosis/stiffness — not iron.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: Which statement about chemical shift liver MRI is correct?
options: Both fat and iron cause signal loss on out-of-phase images
Fat causes signal loss on in-phase images; iron on out-of-phase images
Neither fat nor iron affects signal on chemical shift imaging
Fat causes signal loss on out-of-phase images; iron on in-phase images
Iron increases signal on longer-echo images
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Fat causes signal loss on out-of-phase images; iron on in-phase images
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Fat and water cancel at the out-of-phase echo, so fat drops out there. Iron is paramagnetic and shortens T2*, so signal falls as TE lengthens — worse on the longer-TE in-phase image. "Fat out, iron in."

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 58-year-old has a 2.5 cm right adrenal nodule found incidentally on CT. MRI chemical shift imaging shows the nodule is bright on in-phase images and clearly darker (loses signal) on out-of-phase images. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lipid-rich adenoma
Adrenocortical carcinoma
Phaeochromocytoma
Adrenal metastasis
Myelolipoma
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Signal loss on out-of-phase relative to in-phase imaging indicates intracytoplasmic (microscopic) lipid, characteristic of a benign lipid-rich adenoma. ACC, phaeo and metastasis are lipid-poor and do not drop signal; myelolipoma contains macroscopic fat that behaves differently.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: An adrenal nodule shows NO signal drop on out-of-phase imaging. Which statement is correct?
options: The lesion is definitively malignant and requires urgent resection
The lesion is definitively a benign adenoma
The lesion is indeterminate and needs further work-up such as CT washout
Chemical shift has excluded a phaeochromocytoma
No further assessment of any kind is required
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: The lesion is indeterminate and needs further work-up such as CT washout
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Absence of signal drop means the lesion is lipid-poor and indeterminate — it may be a lipid-poor adenoma, phaeochromocytoma, metastasis, or ACC. It is not automatically malignant, but it warrants further characterisation (e.g. CT washout) and hormonal work-up. Around a third of adenomas are lipid-poor.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 45-year-old with episodic headaches, palpitations and hypertension has a 3 cm adrenal mass that is markedly T2 hyperintense ('light-bulb bright') with no out-of-phase signal drop. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed directly to image-guided biopsy of the mass
Perform urgent adrenalectomy the same day
Start a beta-blocker as first-line to control symptoms
Reassure and discharge as this is a benign adenoma
Measure plasma/urinary metanephrines and arrange alpha-blockade before any intervention
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Measure plasma/urinary metanephrines and arrange alpha-blockade before any intervention
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: The clinical picture and T2 light-bulb appearance strongly suggest phaeochromocytoma. Confirm with metanephrines. Biopsy or surgery on an unblocked phaeo can trigger a hypertensive crisis, so alpha-blockade (then beta-blockade) must precede any intervention. Beta-blockade first risks unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 19-year-old with newly diagnosed Crohn's disease needs cross-sectional imaging of the small bowel, with the expectation of repeated scans over the coming years. Which imaging modality is most appropriate?
options: CT enterography with IV contrast
MR enterography
Abdominal radiograph series
Barium follow-through
Transabdominal ultrasound with oral contrast only
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: MR enterography is preferred for small-bowel Crohn's because it uses no ionising radiation — critical for a young patient needing lifelong monitoring — and gives superior soft-tissue characterisation to separate active inflammation from fibrosis. CT enterography delivers a significant radiation dose that accumulates with repeated scans; barium follow-through is also ionising and less informative about transmural/extraluminal disease.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: During MR enterography, a large volume of a mannitol-based oral solution is administered. What is its primary purpose?
options: To provide an antiperistaltic effect and reduce motion artefact
To act as an intravascular contrast agent for mucosal enhancement
To sterilise the bowel before imaging
To osmotically distend the small-bowel lumen so the wall can be assessed
To restrict diffusion within inflamed segments
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: To osmotically distend the small-bowel lumen so the wall can be assessed
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Mannitol is a non-absorbed osmotic agent that holds fluid in the lumen and distends the bowel, so collapsed loops don't mask or mimic disease. It is biphasic (T2 bright, T1 dark). The antiperistaltic effect comes from IV hyoscine butylbromide/glucagon, and mucosal enhancement from IV gadolinium — not from the oral contrast.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: An MR enterogram shows a narrowed terminal ileal segment with proximal (pre-stenotic) dilatation. The wall shows little post-gadolinium enhancement, no T2 oedema, and no diffusion restriction. What does this most likely represent, and what is the management implication?
options: Predominantly fibrotic stricture — may require surgery or endoscopic dilatation
Active inflammatory stricture — escalate medical therapy with biologics
An abscess requiring urgent drainage
An enterocutaneous fistula requiring stoma formation
Normal terminal ileum — no action needed
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Predominantly fibrotic stricture — may require surgery or endoscopic dilatation
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Absence of enhancement, T2 oedema, and DWI restriction points to fixed fibrosis rather than active inflammation. Fibrotic strictures will not reverse with anti-inflammatory or biologic therapy and, if causing obstruction, are managed surgically or with endoscopic balloon dilatation. Active inflammatory strictures (avid enhancement, oedema, DWI restriction) are treated medically first.

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 42-year-old woman has an incidental renal cyst on ultrasound. MRI shows a cystic lesion with several thick, irregular septa that clearly enhance after gadolinium. Which Bosniak category and management does this indicate?
options: Bosniak I — simple benign cyst, no follow-up needed
Bosniak II — minimally complex, no follow-up needed
Bosniak III — surgical lesion with significant malignant potential
Bosniak IIF — minimally complex, imaging surveillance
Bosniak IV — purely to be managed with reassurance and discharge
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: Bosniak III — surgical lesion with significant malignant potential
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Thick, irregular, enhancing septa define a Bosniak III lesion, which carries significant malignant risk and is managed surgically. Enhancement of walls/septa is the hallmark malignant feature. (Bosniak IV would require an enhancing soft-tissue nodule/solid component; it is also surgical, not discharged.)

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A 60-year-old man with a biopsy-proven renal cell carcinoma is referred for MRI before nephrectomy. Which finding is the most critical for surgical planning that MRI is specifically relied upon to define?
options: The T2 signal characteristics of the primary tumour
The presence of a simple contralateral renal cyst
The degree of perinephric fat present at the lower pole
The renal cortical thickness of the unaffected kidney
The cranial extent of tumour thrombus within the IVC
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.answer: The cranial extent of tumour thrombus within the IVC
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: MRI's unique staging value in RCC is defining the cranial extent of venous tumour thrombus (renal vein/IVC). Whether thrombus is infrahepatic, retrohepatic, or reaches the atrium fundamentally changes the operative approach (potentially requiring cardiopulmonary bypass).

investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.question: A renal lesion shows loss of signal on fat-suppressed sequences and India-ink etching at its margins on opposed-phase imaging. The patient has several similar bilateral lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis and association?
options: Renal cell carcinoma associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease
Angiomyolipoma associated with tuberous sclerosis
Simple cortical cysts associated with ageing
Transitional cell carcinoma associated with smoking
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis associated with staghorn calculi
investigations__MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abd.explanation: Signal drop-out on fat suppression and opposed-phase India-ink artefact indicate macroscopic fat, diagnostic of angiomyolipoma. Multiple bilateral AMLs are strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis. Large AMLs risk haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome).

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: A 32-year-old woman with a known BRCA1 mutation is enrolled in a high-risk surveillance programme. Which imaging modality is the most sensitive for detecting breast cancer in this setting?
options: Mammography alone
Ultrasound alone
Contrast-enhanced dynamic breast MRI
Chest radiograph
Digital breast tomosynthesis alone
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Dynamic gadolinium breast MRI is the most sensitive test for breast cancer and is used for annual screening of high-risk women such as BRCA1 carriers, in whom mammography is inadequate — particularly in young, dense breasts. It carries no ionising radiation, an advantage for repeated imaging in young women.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: On dynamic contrast breast MRI, which kinetic enhancement curve is most suggestive of malignancy?
options: Type 1 — progressive persistent enhancement
Type 2 — plateau enhancement
Type 3 — rapid uptake followed by washout
A curve showing no enhancement at all
Slow, gradual linear enhancement over 8 minutes
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: Type 3 — rapid uptake followed by washout
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Angiogenic cancers show rapid avid gadolinium uptake then washout (a type 3 curve), the hallmark suspicious pattern. Type 1 (persistent) is usually benign and type 2 (plateau) is indeterminate. Curves are assessed together with morphology and reported using BI-RADS.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: Which statement best describes the principal disadvantage of breast MRI relative to mammography?
options: It delivers a high dose of ionising radiation
It cannot image dense breast tissue
It has lower specificity, leading to more false positives and biopsies
It is far cheaper and quicker to perform
It requires no intravenous contrast
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: It has lower specificity, leading to more false positives and biopsies
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: MRI's very high sensitivity is offset by lower specificity: benign parenchyma also enhances, producing false positives, extra recalls and biopsies. It is also costly, needs gadolinium contrast, and involves MRI safety considerations — hence it is usually combined with mammography in surveillance.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: To reduce background parenchymal enhancement and improve accuracy, when should breast MRI ideally be scheduled in a pre-menopausal woman?
options: Days 1–3 of the cycle (during menstruation)
Days 7–14 of the cycle (follicular phase)
Days 21–28 of the cycle (luteal phase)
Only during ovulation
Timing has no effect on the images
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Background parenchymal enhancement is lowest in the follicular phase (roughly days 7–14), so scanning then reduces false positives and makes suspicious lesions easier to detect. This cycle-timing is a practical requirement unique to pre-menopausal women.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: A 54-year-old woman has an invasive ductal carcinoma confirmed on core biopsy after triple assessment. Which statement best describes the role of breast MRI at this point?
options: It is required routinely for every newly diagnosed breast cancer to confirm the histological subtype
It replaces mammography and ultrasound for staging the local disease
It is a selective problem-solving tool used to refine surgical planning in specific situations
It is used to make the initial diagnosis in place of core biopsy
It is contraindicated once a cancer has already been diagnosed
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: It is a selective problem-solving tool used to refine surgical planning in specific situations
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: MRI has no role in making the diagnosis (triple assessment does that) and does not replace mammography/US. Once cancer is confirmed it is used selectively to answer surgical questions such as extent, multifocality and neoadjuvant response — not routinely for all patients.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: Which histological type of breast cancer is a classic indication for MRI because it is frequently mammographically occult and has its extent underestimated by conventional imaging?
options: Invasive lobular carcinoma
Invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type
Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma
Ductal carcinoma in situ, low grade
Tubular carcinoma
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Invasive lobular carcinoma grows in a diffuse, single-file pattern that is often occult or size-underestimated on mammography. MRI defines its true extent far better, which is why it is a recognised indication for pre-operative MRI.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: During pre-operative MRI for a planned wide local excision, an unexpected small enhancing focus is seen in a separate quadrant. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed directly to mastectomy based on the MRI finding
Ignore the finding as MRI enhancement is always benign
Obtain histological confirmation, usually via second-look ultrasound and targeted biopsy, before changing the surgical plan
Start neoadjuvant chemotherapy immediately
Repeat the MRI in six months without further action
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: Obtain histological confirmation, usually via second-look ultrasound and targeted biopsy, before changing the surgical plan
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: MRI can detect incidental benign enhancement and overestimate disease. An additional lesion must be biopsy-confirmed before escalating surgery — converting to mastectomy on MRI alone risks overtreatment without survival benefit.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: A 54-year-old woman with silicone breast implants has MRI showing multiple wavy, low-signal curvilinear lines floating within the silicone, but the fibrous capsule appears intact. What is the diagnosis?
options: Normal radial folds
Intracapsular rupture (linguine sign)
Extracapsular rupture
Capsular contracture
Gel bleed
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Wavy low-signal lines (the collapsed shell) suspended in silicone with an intact fibrous capsule is the linguine sign, pathognomonic of intracapsular rupture. The silicone remains contained within the capsule.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: Which statement about MRI assessment of silicone implant integrity is correct?
options: IV gadolinium contrast is essential to detect rupture
Silicone-specific sequences are used and no contrast is required
Ultrasound is superior to MRI for shell integrity
Radial folds indicate rupture and mandate explant
Saline implants require silicone-selective sequences to detect deflation
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: Silicone-specific sequences are used and no contrast is required
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: MRI is the best test for silicone implant integrity using silicone-selective/water-suppressed sequences; no contrast is needed. Radial folds are normal, and saline implant rupture is seen as visible deflation without special sequences.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: An 8-months-post-op... a woman presents 3 years after textured implant insertion with a new peri-implant fluid collection. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and rescan in 5 years
Immediate bilateral explant without further tests
Aspirate the fluid and send for cytology and CD30
Start empirical antibiotics for infection
Diagnose intracapsular rupture and observe
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: Aspirate the fluid and send for cytology and CD30
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: A new late peri-implant seroma around a textured implant must raise suspicion of BIA-ALCL. The correct step is ultrasound-guided aspiration with fluid sent for cytology and CD30 immunostaining, not observation or blind explant.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: A 54-year-old woman presents with a firm right axillary lymph node. Core biopsy shows metastatic adenocarcinoma that is ER-positive, PR-positive and GATA3-positive. Bilateral mammography and whole-breast ultrasound are normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat mammography in 6 months
Contrast-enhanced breast MRI
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis only
Bilateral mastectomy
Reassurance and discharge
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: The picture is an occult breast primary: breast-type nodal adenocarcinoma (ER/PR/GATA3 positive) with negative mammography and ultrasound. Contrast-enhanced breast MRI is highly sensitive and identifies the occult primary in the majority of cases, enabling targeted biopsy and breast conservation.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: In a patient with a proven occult breast primary, why is locating the tumour on MRI clinically important?
options: It confirms the node is benign
It allows breast-conserving surgery and targeted treatment instead of empirical whole-breast radiotherapy or mastectomy
It removes the need for any surgery
It replaces the need for histological receptor testing
It rules out distant metastatic disease
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: It allows breast-conserving surgery and targeted treatment instead of empirical whole-breast radiotherapy or mastectomy
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: When no primary is found, patients are often treated with whole-breast radiotherapy or mastectomy for presumed disease. Finding the primary permits precise, breast-conserving surgery and tailored adjuvant therapy, and refines staging.

investigations__MRI__Breast.question: A woman is due to undergo gadolinium-enhanced breast MRI to search for an occult primary. Which statement is correct regarding safety and technique?
options: Renal function need not be checked before gadolinium
High-risk gadolinium agents are preferred in severe renal impairment
Imaging is ideally performed on days 7-14 of the menstrual cycle to reduce background parenchymal enhancement
MRI-incompatible implants do not need screening
Pregnancy status is irrelevant to the scan
investigations__MRI__Breast.answer: Imaging is ideally performed on days 7-14 of the menstrual cycle to reduce background parenchymal enhancement
investigations__MRI__Breast.explanation: Scanning in the second week of the cycle minimises hormonally-driven background enhancement that can mask a small primary. Renal function must be checked (high-risk agents avoided in severe impairment due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), implants/devices screened, and pregnancy asked about.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 42-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and two first-degree relatives who had "brain bleeds" is referred for elective intracranial aneurysm screening. She has no symptoms and normal renal function. Which imaging investigation is most appropriate first-line?
options: Non-contrast CT head
Time-of-flight MR angiography
Digital subtraction angiography
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI brain with contrast
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: For asymptomatic elective aneurysm screening (e.g. ADPKD, family history), non-contrast TOF-MRA is the preferred first-line test — no radiation, no contrast. DSA is invasive and reserved for characterisation/treatment; CT and LP belong to the acute SAH pathway.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 55-year-old man presents with a sudden "worst-ever" headache that peaked within seconds, with neck stiffness. What is the correct initial imaging pathway?
options: Time-of-flight MRA of the Circle of Willis
Non-contrast CT head, then CT angiography if aneurysm suspected
Contrast-enhanced MRI brain
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Reassure and arrange outpatient MRA
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Non-contrast CT head, then CT angiography if aneurysm suspected
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: This is a thunderclap headache — subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Immediate non-contrast CT head is first; if negative, LP for xanthochromia, and CTA/DSA to find the aneurysm. Elective MRA is not the acute pathway.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: On a TOF-MRA an intracranial vessel appears to show a very tight, near-complete stenosis. Which statement best reflects a recognised limitation of the technique?
options: TOF underestimates stenosis because slow flow appears bright
TOF cannot image the posterior circulation
TOF requires gadolinium, so contrast reactions cause artefact
TOF can overestimate stenosis because turbulent/slow flow causes signal loss
TOF is unaffected by patient motion
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: TOF can overestimate stenosis because turbulent/slow flow causes signal loss
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: Turbulent or slow flow causes spin dephasing and signal loss, so TOF-MRA tends to overestimate the degree of stenosis (or make a near-occlusion look complete). It is also motion-sensitive. Confirm with CTA or DSA when it will alter management.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 68-year-old man has a right-sided TIA. Duplex suggests a tight left internal carotid stenosis and a moderate right stenosis. MRA confirms 80% stenosis on the right and 65% on the left. Which lesion most warrants urgent carotid endarterectomy?
options: The left carotid, because it is the tighter absolute stenosis
The right carotid, because it is symptomatic (ipsilateral to the TIA)
Neither, as both are below the treatment threshold
The left carotid, because bilateral disease is treated left-first
Both simultaneously in one operation
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: The right carotid, because it is symptomatic (ipsilateral to the TIA)
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: Benefit from endarterectomy is greatest for symptomatic stenosis on the side ipsilateral to the ischaemic event. A right-sided TIA localises to the right carotid; its 80% symptomatic stenosis is the priority, done within ~2 weeks.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with left neck pain, partial left ptosis and miosis, and transient right arm weakness after a yoga session. Which finding on neck MRI/MRA best supports the likely diagnosis?
options: Atheromatous calcified plaque at the carotid bifurcation
A bright crescent of intramural haematoma on fat-saturated T1
Diffuse small-vessel white matter change
Bilateral vertebral artery hypoplasia
A berry aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: A bright crescent of intramural haematoma on fat-saturated T1
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: A young patient with neck pain, a painful Horner's syndrome and cerebral ischaemia after neck movement suggests carotid dissection. The crescent sign — bright methaemoglobin in the wall on fat-sat T1 — is the classic finding; atheroma would be unusual at this age.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: Regarding MRA safety and technique in carotid imaging, which statement is correct?
options: Gadolinium contrast can be given freely regardless of renal function
TOF-MRA reliably underestimates the degree of stenosis
Pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants must be screened for before MRI
CE-MRA is contraindicated in all patients with metallic dental fillings
MRA uses ionising radiation and cumulative dose must be tracked
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants must be screened for before MRI
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: MRI safety screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic/cochlear implants is essential. MRI uses no ionising radiation; gadolinium is used cautiously in severe renal impairment (NSF risk); TOF tends to overestimate, not underestimate, stenosis.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 28-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum, presents with a worsening headache and a focal seizure. CT shows a right parietal haemorrhage that crosses arterial territory boundaries. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Digital subtraction cerebral angiography for aneurysm
MR venography (MRV)
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
Repeat non-contrast CT in 24 hours
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: A haemorrhagic infarct crossing arterial territories in a peripartum woman with headache and seizure is the classic picture of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. MRV (or CT venography) is the key test, demonstrating absent flow in the affected sinus.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A patient with confirmed superior sagittal sinus thrombosis has a small associated venous haemorrhagic infarct. What is the recommended management?
options: Withhold all anticoagulation because of the haemorrhage
Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH or heparin
Intravenous mannitol alone
Immediate surgical evacuation of the haematoma
Aspirin monotherapy only
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH or heparin
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: CVST is treated with anticoagulation even in the presence of venous haemorrhagic infarction — the bleed results from venous obstruction, and treating the clot is the priority. The underlying prothrombotic cause should also be sought.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: On a contrast-enhanced scan of a patient with headache and papilloedema, a triangular non-enhancing filling defect is seen within the enhancing walls of the superior sagittal sinus. What does this sign represent?
options: A normal arachnoid granulation
The empty delta sign of sinus thrombosis
An enhancing meningioma
A hypoplastic transverse sinus variant
Cortical laminar necrosis
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: The empty delta sign of sinus thrombosis
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: The empty delta (or empty triangle) sign is non-enhancing thrombus surrounded by enhancing dura in the superior sagittal sinus and indicates sinus thrombosis. Arachnoid granulations are rounded, and a hypoplastic transverse sinus is a different, unilateral flow variant.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 34-year-old woman has resistant hypertension. MRA shows a "string of beads" appearance in the mid-to-distal segment of the right renal artery. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate first-line intervention?
options: Atherosclerotic RAS; lifelong medical therapy only
Fibromuscular dysplasia; balloon angioplasty
Renal artery aneurysm; open surgical repair
Polyarteritis nodosa; high-dose corticosteroids
Takayasu arteritis; renal artery stenting
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: A young woman with a mid/distal "string of beads" appearance has fibromuscular dysplasia, which characteristically responds well to plain balloon angioplasty, unlike ostial atherosclerotic disease.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 70-year-old man with bilateral atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is started on ramipril for hypertension. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen sharply. What is the mechanism?
options: Direct nephrotoxicity of the ACE inhibitor on tubular cells
Loss of angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, reducing glomerular filtration pressure
Acute interstitial nephritis from the drug
Rhabdomyolysis precipitated by the medication
Contrast-induced nephropathy from prior imaging
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Loss of angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, reducing glomerular filtration pressure
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: In bilateral RAS, filtration depends on angiotensin-II-driven efferent arteriolar tone. RAAS blockade removes this, dropping intraglomerular pressure and causing acute kidney injury — the classic creatinine rise after ACE inhibitor/ARB.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: When imaging a patient with severe renal impairment for suspected renal artery stenosis, which is the most important contrast-related safety consideration?
options: Iodinated contrast allergy causing anaphylaxis
Gadolinium causing nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Barium aspiration during the scan
Radiation dose to the kidneys
Contrast extravasation at the injection site
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: MRA uses gadolinium, not iodinated contrast, and involves no ionising radiation. In severe renal impairment gadolinium is associated with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, so non-contrast MRA techniques or alternative imaging are preferred.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 68-year-old man has right calf claudication after 100 m. ABPI is 0.7. CE-MRA run-off shows a single 3 cm focal occlusion of the superficial femoral artery with good distal reconstitution. What is the most appropriate revascularisation strategy?
options: Femoropopliteal bypass graft
Percutaneous angioplasty ± stent of the focal lesion
Primary amputation
Long-term warfarin alone
Immediate CT to exclude dissection
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Percutaneous angioplasty ± stent of the focal lesion
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: Short, focal stenoses or occlusions with good run-off are ideally treated endovascularly with angioplasty ± stenting. Bypass is reserved for long-segment occlusions. There is no indication for amputation or dissection imaging here.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 55-year-old woman with an iodinated-contrast allergy needs peripheral arterial mapping. Which single factor most strongly limits the use of gadolinium-enhanced MRA in this decision?
options: Presence of intermittent claudication
Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30)
A calcified abdominal aorta
Prior lower-limb angioplasty
Age under 60
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: Gadolinium is associated with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment, so renal function must be checked before CE-MRA. Contrast allergy actually favours MRA over iodinated CT; the other options do not contraindicate it.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: A 72-year-old man presents with a sudden, painful, cold, pale, pulseless right leg with new paraesthesia. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Arrange urgent CE-MRA run-off before any treatment
Give IV heparin and refer for emergency revascularisation
Prescribe supervised exercise therapy
Measure ABPI and review in clinic in 2 weeks
Start a statin and aspirin and discharge
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Give IV heparin and refer for emergency revascularisation
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: This is acute limb ischaemia (the 6 Ps) — a surgical emergency. Immediate IV heparin and urgent revascularisation are required; you must NOT delay for MRA. Exercise therapy and outpatient review apply to stable claudication, not acute ischaemia.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: Regarding imaging of suspected ACUTE aortic dissection, why is CT angiography generally preferred over MRA?
options: CT avoids all ionising radiation
CT is faster and more readily available for unstable patients
MRA cannot demonstrate an intimal flap
MRA uses iodinated contrast that is nephrotoxic
CT requires no contrast at all
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: CT is faster and more readily available for unstable patients
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: CT angiography is quicker and more accessible, which is decisive in acute, potentially unstable dissection. MRA can show the flap and true/false lumens but is slower. Note CT does use ionising radiation and iodinated contrast — it is MRA that avoids both.

investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.question: Before a patient undergoes MRA, which safety check is essential?
options: Confirm the patient has fasted for 12 hours
Screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and metallic foreign bodies
Measure serum potassium
Stop all antiplatelet drugs 5 days beforehand
Perform a chest radiograph in every patient
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.answer: Screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and metallic foreign bodies
investigations__MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV.explanation: MRI safety screening for non-MR-conditional devices and ferromagnetic material is mandatory before any MR scan. Prolonged fasting, potassium levels, stopping antiplatelets and routine chest films are not standard prerequisites for MRA.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 64-year-old man with a PSA of 8 ng/mL undergoes mpMRI before biopsy. A 1.2 cm focus in the left peripheral zone shows low T2 signal, marked restriction on DWI with low ADC, and early enhancement. Which sequence is the primary determinant of the PI-RADS score for this lesion?
options: T2-weighted imaging
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI/ADC)
Dynamic contrast enhancement
T1-weighted imaging
Gradient-echo susceptibility imaging
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: In the peripheral zone, DWI/ADC is the dominant sequence for PI-RADS scoring. In the transition zone, T2-weighted imaging is dominant. DCE acts as a tie-breaker.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A man with a raised PSA has an mpMRI reported as PI-RADS 4 in the right peripheral zone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat PSA in 12 months
Proceed to targeted MRI-fusion biopsy and discuss at MDT
Start empirical antibiotics for prostatitis
Immediate radical prostatectomy without biopsy
Commence androgen deprivation therapy
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Proceed to targeted MRI-fusion biopsy and discuss at MDT
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: PI-RADS 4 indicates a high likelihood of clinically significant cancer. This warrants histological confirmation via targeted (fusion) biopsy and MDT discussion, not reassurance or blind treatment.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 70-year-old man with known prostate cancer and bone metastases develops severe new lower back pain with leg weakness and urinary retention. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Outpatient lumbar spine X-ray
Urgent whole-spine MRI and dexamethasone
Oral analgesia and physiotherapy referral
Repeat PSA and bone scan in one week
Pelvic mpMRI to reassess the primary
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: This is metastatic spinal cord compression, an oncological emergency. Immediate high-dose dexamethasone and urgent whole-spine MRI are required to preserve neurological function before definitive radiotherapy or surgery.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: On prostate mpMRI, which finding would most strongly favour radiotherapy or non-nerve-sparing surgery over a nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy?
options: A well-defined transition-zone nodule
Seminal vesicle invasion with extracapsular extension
High peripheral-zone T2 signal
A simple prostatic cyst
Diffuse benign prostatic hyperplasia
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Seminal vesicle invasion with extracapsular extension
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Extracapsular extension and seminal vesicle invasion indicate non-organ-confined disease and involvement near the neurovascular bundle, arguing against nerve-sparing surgery and favouring radiotherapy or wider resection.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A well-defined nodule is seen in the transition zone of the prostate on mpMRI. Which is the most likely benign explanation, and which sequence is dominant for scoring lesions in this zone?
options: Benign prostatic hyperplasia; T2-weighted dominant
Prostatitis; DCE dominant
Bone metastasis; DWI dominant
Seminal vesicle cyst; T1 dominant
Urethral stricture; DWI dominant
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: BPH arises in the transition zone and forms well-defined nodules that should not be over-called as cancer. In the transition zone, T2-weighted imaging is the dominant sequence for PI-RADS scoring.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 34-year-old woman with heavy periods has an ultrasound showing a bulky uterus but no discrete mass. MRI shows diffuse thickening of the junctional zone to 15 mm with scattered small T2-hyperintense foci and ill-defined margins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Submucosal fibroid
Adenomyosis
Endometrial carcinoma
Endometrioma
Bicornuate uterus
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Diffuse junctional-zone thickening >12 mm with small T2-bright foci and an ill-defined, globular uterus is the hallmark of adenomyosis. A fibroid would be a focal, sharply-marginated dark-T2 mass rather than diffuse thickening.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 28-year-old woman with chronic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhoea has an ovarian cyst. On MRI it is markedly hyperintense on T1, remains bright on T1 fat-saturated images, and shows dependent T2 shading. What is the diagnosis?
options: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)
Simple functional cyst
Endometrioma
Serous cystadenoma
Fibroid undergoing red degeneration
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: An endometrioma contains old blood, so it is T1 hyperintense and does NOT suppress on fat-sat (a dermoid's fat WOULD suppress), and shows T2 shading. These features distinguish it from dermoids, functional cysts and cystadenomas.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A woman with symptomatic fibroids is being assessed for uterine artery embolisation. What is the single most important reason MRI is performed before the procedure?
options: To measure bone mineral density of the pelvis
To map the number, size and location of fibroids and confirm suitability for embolisation
To deliver therapeutic radiation to the fibroids
To screen for osteoporosis before surgery
To assess fetal wellbeing
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: To map the number, size and location of fibroids and confirm suitability for embolisation
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: MRI provides an anatomical map (number, size, FIGO location, viability/enhancement) that guides whether myomectomy or UAE is appropriate and flags features such as pedunculated subserosal lesions that are a relative UAE contraindication. MRI uses no ionising radiation.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: Which MRI finding in a patient with deep infiltrating endometriosis should prompt formal gynaecology MDT planning rather than routine excision?
options: A single 3 cm subserosal fibroid
A T1-bright endometrioma that suppresses on fat-sat
Ureteric involvement causing hydronephrosis
A normal junctional zone of 6 mm
A convex fundal contour
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Deep endometriosis involving the ureter (with hydronephrosis) or bowel requires multidisciplinary planning because resection carries significant risk. An endometrioma that suppresses on fat-sat would actually argue against endometrioma, and the other options are benign/normal.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 52-year-old woman with biopsy-proven cervical squamous cell carcinoma undergoes staging MRI. The low-signal cervical stromal ring is disrupted with tumour signal extending into the parametrial fat. What is the most important management implication?
options: Simple hysterectomy remains the treatment of choice
Radical trachelectomy to preserve fertility is now indicated
She should be managed with chemoradiotherapy rather than primary surgery
No further staging is required as the tumour is early stage
Cone biopsy alone is sufficient treatment
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: She should be managed with chemoradiotherapy rather than primary surgery
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Loss of the intact low-signal stromal ring with tumour in parametrial fat indicates parametrial invasion. This upstages the disease and moves the patient from a surgical pathway to chemoradiotherapy — the pivotal decision MRI informs in cervical cancer.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: MRI is performed for staging endometrial adenocarcinoma. Which single MRI finding is the key factor guiding whether lymphadenectomy is performed?
options: Endometrial cavity distension
Depth of myometrial invasion (<50% vs ≥50%)
Presence of a fibroid
Junctional zone thickness alone
Volume of endometrial fluid
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Depth of myometrial invasion is the key prognostic and staging factor. Invasion ≥50% carries a higher risk of nodal spread and guides the decision to perform lymphadenectomy.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 66-year-old woman reports a single episode of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Reassure her as bleeding is common after menopause
Investigate as endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, starting with transvaginal ultrasound and biopsy
Proceed directly to staging MRI without tissue diagnosis
Start hormone replacement therapy
Arrange PET-CT as the first-line investigation
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Investigate as endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, starting with transvaginal ultrasound and biopsy
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding must be treated as endometrial cancer until excluded. First-line assessment is transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness, with endometrial biopsy/hysteroscopy for tissue diagnosis. MRI is reserved for local staging once cancer is confirmed.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 62-year-old man has a mid-rectal adenocarcinoma. On staging MRI the tumour extends into the perirectal fat and its outer edge lies 0.5 mm from the mesorectal fascia. What is the most important management consequence of this finding?
options: Proceed directly to total mesorectal excision without further treatment
Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to downstage the tumour and clear the margin before surgery
Immediate abdominoperineal resection with permanent stoma
Palliative care referral as the tumour is inoperable
Endoscopic mucosal resection alone
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to downstage the tumour and clear the margin before surgery
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Tumour ≤1 mm from the mesorectal fascia means a threatened/involved circumferential resection margin (CRM). This predicts high local recurrence if resected immediately, so the patient is given neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to shrink the tumour and achieve a clear TME margin. The tumour is not inoperable, and depth into fat alone does not mandate APR.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: On a rectal cancer MRI report, tumour is described as extending through the muscularis propria into the perirectal fat but not into any adjacent organ. Which T-stage does this represent?
options: T1
T2
T3
T4a
T4b
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: T3 is invasion through the muscularis propria into the perirectal (mesorectal) fat. T1/T2 remain confined to the wall. T4a is breach of the peritoneal surface and T4b is invasion of an adjacent organ — neither is present here.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: Which MRI feature is the strongest indicator that a mesorectal lymph node is malignant in rectal cancer staging?
options: A node measuring greater than 5 mm in short axis
An irregular spiculated border with mixed heterogeneous signal
A smooth round node with homogeneous low signal
Any node visible within the mesorectum
A node located more than 3 cm from the primary tumour
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: An irregular spiculated border with mixed heterogeneous signal
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Nodal assessment on rectal MRI relies on morphology rather than size: an irregular/spiculated border and mixed heterogeneous internal signal (with round shape) are the most reliable predictors of malignancy. Size alone is unreliable — small nodes can be involved and large nodes can be reactive.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 34-year-old man has a recurrent perianal fistula. MRI shows a tract crossing both the internal and external anal sphincter into the ischioanal fossa. Which Parks type is this?
options: Intersphincteric
Transsphincteric
Suprasphincteric
Extrasphincteric
Submucosal
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: A transsphincteric fistula crosses both the internal and external sphincter to reach the ischioanal fossa. Intersphincteric crosses only the internal sphincter; suprasphincteric loops over puborectalis; extrasphincteric bypasses the sphincter complex entirely.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: On a dedicated anal fistula MRI protocol, which finding best indicates an ACTIVE fistula tract?
options: Low signal throughout the tract on all sequences
High T2/STIR signal with enhancement of the tract wall after gadolinium
Absence of any enhancement after gadolinium
Fat signal within the tract that suppresses on STIR
Gas locules with no surrounding change
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: High T2/STIR signal with enhancement of the tract wall after gadolinium
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: An active tract contains fluid (bright on T2/STIR) and is lined by vascular granulation tissue that enhances with gadolinium. A purely fibrotic, inactive tract is low signal and enhances little.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with severe perianal pain, systemic sepsis and crepitus over the perineum. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Urgent MRI pelvis before any intervention
Urgent surgical debridement/incision and drainage with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Outpatient colorectal referral for elective fistula surgery
Commence a biologic agent for presumed Crohn's disease
Discharge with oral antibiotics and review in two weeks
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Urgent surgical debridement/incision and drainage with broad-spectrum antibiotics
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: This is Fournier's gangrene (necrotising perineal sepsis), a surgical emergency in diabetic/immunocompromised patients. It requires immediate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement — you do not delay for MRI.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: MRI of a young woman with multiple, branching perianal fistulae and features of proctitis most strongly suggests which underlying diagnosis?
options: Simple cryptoglandular fistula
Crohn's disease
Ulcerative colitis
Diverticular disease
Irritable bowel syndrome
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Multiple, complex or branching fistulae with proctitis point to perianal Crohn's disease, which requires combined medical and surgical MDT management. Ulcerative colitis rarely causes fistulae; a single simple tract is typically cryptoglandular.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: For which MRI finding is a simple fistulotomy (laying open the tract) generally the SAFEST surgical option?
options: A high transsphincteric tract crossing most of the external sphincter
A suprasphincteric tract with supralevator extension
A low intersphincteric tract crossing minimal sphincter
A complex fistula with a horseshoe extension
An extrasphincteric fistula in Crohn's disease
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: A low intersphincteric tract crossing minimal sphincter
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Fistulotomy divides the tissue overlying the tract, so it is only safe when little sphincter is crossed, as in a low intersphincteric fistula. High, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric or complex/Crohn's tracts risk incontinence and need sphincter-preserving techniques.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 34-year-old woman has a 5 cm left adnexal cyst that is indeterminate on transvaginal ultrasound. Pelvic MRI shows the lesion is uniformly hyperintense on T1 and remains bright on fat-saturated sequences, with low signal ('shading') on T2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)
Endometrioma
Simple functional cyst
Ovarian fibroma
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: T1 hyperintensity that does NOT suppress on fat-sat indicates blood (not fat), and low-signal 'T2 shading' is the classic endometrioma fingerprint. A dermoid would lose signal on fat-sat (macroscopic fat); a simple cyst is T2 bright with no shading; a fibroma is very low T2 and solid; carcinoma shows enhancing solid tissue.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: MRI of an adnexal mass shows a T1-bright component that loses signal on fat-saturated imaging, together with a small mural (Rokitansky) nodule. Which lesion does this describe?
options: Endometrioma
Serous cystadenocarcinoma
Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)
Fibrothecoma
Haemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: Signal dropout on fat-sat/chemical-shift proves macroscopic fat, the hallmark of a mature cystic teratoma; a Rokitansky (dermoid) nodule further supports it. Blood-containing lesions (endometrioma, haemorrhagic cyst) stay bright on fat-sat, a fibrothecoma is very low T2, and carcinoma shows enhancing solid tissue.

investigations__MRI__Pelvis.question: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has a large complex left ovarian mass. MRI shows avidly enhancing solid components, thick irregular septa with papillary projections, and moderate ascites. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 12 months
Refer to the gynae-oncology MDT as suspected ovarian malignancy
Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive to suppress the cyst
Arrange outpatient laparoscopic cystectomy by general gynaecology
Start empirical antibiotics for a tubo-ovarian abscess
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.answer: Refer to the gynae-oncology MDT as suspected ovarian malignancy
investigations__MRI__Pelvis.explanation: A complex, solid, enhancing adnexal mass with ascites is ovarian malignancy until proven otherwise and must be referred to the gynae-oncology MDT for staging (adding CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) and surgical planning. Conservative follow-up, hormonal suppression, routine general-gynae cystectomy, or antibiotics would all inappropriately delay cancer management.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A 68-year-old man with fatigue, bone pain and renal impairment has a monoclonal paraprotein. According to NICE, what is the recommended first-line whole-body imaging for suspected multiple myeloma?
options: Plain-film skeletal survey
Whole-body MRI (including diffusion-weighted imaging)
Radionuclide (technetium) bone scan
Plain chest and pelvic radiographs only
DEXA bone densitometry
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: NICE recommends WB-MRI (or whole-body DWI) as first-line whole-body imaging for suspected myeloma because it is far more sensitive for marrow disease than the old skeletal survey, detecting lesions before lytic bone destruction is visible.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A patient with biopsy-proven multiple myeloma and widespread bone pain has a technetium bone scan reported as normal. What best explains this?
options: The dose of radiotracer was too low
Myeloma is purely lytic/osteoclastic and produces little osteoblastic activity
Bone scans cannot image the vertebral column
The lesions are too small to detect by any modality
The patient moved during acquisition
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: Myeloma is purely lytic/osteoclastic and produces little osteoblastic activity
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Bone scans depend on osteoblastic (bone-forming) uptake. Myeloma is a lytic, osteoclast-driven process with minimal reactive new bone, so it is classically falsely negative on bone scan — assess it with WB-MRI or CT instead.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: On whole-body MRI, which signal pattern indicates tumour replacing normal fatty bone marrow?
options: Bright on T1, dark on STIR and DWI
Dark on T1, bright on STIR and high-b DWI
Bright on all sequences equally
Dark on all sequences equally
No change from surrounding normal marrow on any sequence
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: Dark on T1, bright on STIR and high-b DWI
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Normal adult marrow is fatty and bright on T1. Tumour replacement of that fat makes the marrow dark on T1 and bright on the water-sensitive, fat-suppressed STIR and high-b diffusion sequences — the core marrow-replacement signature.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A 68-year-old presents with sudden right-sided weakness 40 minutes ago. Non-contrast CT head is normal. MRI shows a left frontal region that is bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map. What does this indicate?
options: Chronic small-vessel ischaemic change
T2 shine-through artefact
Acute ischaemic infarction
Vasogenic oedema from a tumour
Normal appearance
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Bright DWI with dark (low) ADC is true restricted diffusion from cytotoxic oedema — the earliest, most sensitive sign of acute infarction, positive within minutes and before CT changes. This patient should enter the acute stroke/reperfusion pathway.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A lesion is bright on DWI. Which single finding best confirms it represents TRUE restricted diffusion rather than T2 shine-through?
options: It is also bright on T2/FLAIR
The ADC map is dark (low signal)
The ADC map is bright (high signal)
It enhances with gadolinium
It is dark on T1
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: The ADC map is dark (low signal)
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: DWI is built on a T2 image, so a T2-bright lesion can shine through as bright DWI without restriction. The ADC map is the arbiter: true restriction is DARK on ADC; shine-through is bright/normal on ADC.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A ring-enhancing intracranial lesion is found. Which DWI finding most supports a pyogenic abscess rather than a necrotic high-grade tumour?
options: The centre of the lesion shows restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC)
The centre shows no restriction with bright ADC
The rim is dark on DWI
The lesion is bright on T1 before contrast
There is no diffusion signal anywhere
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: The centre of the lesion shows restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC)
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Viscous, cellular pus in an abscess cavity restricts diffusion, giving a bright DWI and dark ADC centre. The necrotic core of a tumour typically does not restrict — a key discriminator in the exam and on the ward.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: Which physiological change underlies the BOLD signal that fMRI detects in an activated cortical region?
options: A direct electrical recording of neuronal action potentials
Increased local blood flow delivering excess oxyhaemoglobin, reducing paramagnetic deoxyhaemoglobin
Accumulation of paramagnetic oxyhaemoglobin that increases field distortion
Gadolinium contrast leaking across a disrupted blood-brain barrier
A drop in regional cerebral blood flow to active neurons
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: Increased local blood flow delivering excess oxyhaemoglobin, reducing paramagnetic deoxyhaemoglobin
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Neuronal activity triggers a local increase in blood flow that over-supplies oxyhaemoglobin (diamagnetic) and washes out deoxyhaemoglobin (paramagnetic). This lowers field distortion and raises the T2*-weighted BOLD signal. It is indirect and haemodynamic, not a direct electrical recording, and does not depend on gadolinium.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A 45-year-old is due for resection of a glioma in the left frontal lobe. Which is the single most appropriate role of fMRI in her management?
options: Confirming the histological grade of the tumour
Mapping eloquent language cortex adjacent to the lesion to guide the resection margin
Detecting acute intratumoural haemorrhage
Measuring cerebral perfusion to diagnose stroke
Screening the whole brain for occult metastases
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: Mapping eloquent language cortex adjacent to the lesion to guide the resection margin
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: fMRI's main clinical use is pre-surgical planning: identifying eloquent cortex (here, left-sided language areas such as Broca's) next to the tumour so the surgeon can resect while minimising post-operative deficit. It does not grade tumours, detect haemorrhage, or screen for metastases — those are other imaging/pathology roles.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: Which statement about fMRI is correct?
options: It has higher temporal resolution than EEG
It directly records neuronal electrical activity
Oxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic and deoxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic
Resting-state fMRI can assess functional connectivity without the patient performing a task
It is a routine first-line clinical investigation for headache
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: Resting-state fMRI can assess functional connectivity without the patient performing a task
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Resting-state fMRI uses spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations to map functional networks without any task, which is useful when patients cannot cooperate. fMRI has LOWER temporal resolution than EEG, is an indirect (not direct electrical) measure, oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic while deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic, and it is a specialised rather than routine test.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A 26-week fetus has isolated ventriculomegaly on ultrasound. Fetal MRI is arranged for further characterisation. Which statement about the choice of MRI here is correct?
options: MRI is the first-line screening test for fetal anomalies
Intravenous gadolinium should be given to improve brain contrast
MRI is used as a second-line problem-solving test after ultrasound
MRI is preferred because ultrasound involves ionising radiation
MRI must be delayed until after delivery to be safe
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: MRI is used as a second-line problem-solving test after ultrasound
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Ultrasound is first-line for fetal assessment; MRI is second-line to characterise an abnormality US has already found — here, to seek associated anomalies such as agenesis of the corpus callosum. Gadolinium is avoided as it crosses the placenta, and neither US nor MRI uses ionising radiation.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: Why is gadolinium contrast avoided in fetal MRI?
options: It is ferromagnetic and heats the fetus
It crosses the placenta and enters the fetal/amniotic compartment
It causes ionising radiation exposure to the fetus
It is only avoided in the first trimester and safe later
It prevents the amniotic fluid from providing contrast
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: It crosses the placenta and enters the fetal/amniotic compartment
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: Gadolinium crosses the placenta, is excreted into amniotic fluid and recirculates, and is associated with adverse fetal outcomes, so fetal MRI is performed without contrast. MRI itself uses no ionising radiation, and gadolinium is avoided throughout pregnancy.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A fetus has a large anterior neck mass on ultrasound that appears to threaten the airway. Fetal MRI is requested. What is the main way MRI alters management?
options: It confirms the mass is benign so no intervention is needed
It allows planning of an EXIT procedure to secure the airway at delivery
It replaces the need for a fetal-medicine MDT discussion
It is used to deliver gadolinium directly to the mass
It determines the fetal karyotype
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: It allows planning of an EXIT procedure to secure the airway at delivery
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: MRI defines the extent of an airway-threatening neck mass and its relationship to the airway, enabling the fetal-medicine MDT to plan an EXIT (ex-utero intrapartum treatment) procedure, securing the airway while the fetus remains on placental circulation. It does not give contrast or determine karyotype.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: A neurosurgeon requests DTI tractography before resecting a left peri-Rolandic glioma. On the colour-coded fibre map, the corticospinal tract adjacent to the tumour is displayed in blue. What does the blue colour indicate about the fibres' orientation?
options: The fibres run predominantly left–right (transverse)
The fibres run predominantly anterior–posterior
The fibres run predominantly superior–inferior (cranio-caudal)
The fibres have low fractional anisotropy and are disorganised
The fibres contain CSF and diffuse isotropically
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: By the standard DTI convention, blue encodes superior–inferior orientation, green anterior–posterior, and red left–right. The corticospinal tract runs cranio-caudally and is therefore blue — consistent, not incidental, and it is the pathway the surgeon must preserve to avoid a motor deficit.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: Which statement about fractional anisotropy (FA) is correct?
options: High FA indicates disrupted, damaged white-matter tracts
FA measures grey-matter metabolic activity
Reduced FA is highly specific for demyelination and excludes other causes
High FA indicates organised, intact white-matter tracts; reduced FA suggests tract disruption
FA can only be calculated in cerebrospinal fluid
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: High FA indicates organised, intact white-matter tracts; reduced FA suggests tract disruption
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: FA quantifies how directional (anisotropic) diffusion is at a voxel and serves as a marker of tract integrity. High FA reflects well-organised intact fibres; reduced FA reflects loss of organisation from damage or demyelination. It is sensitive but non-specific — it cannot by itself distinguish the underlying cause.

investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.question: Which of the following is a recognised limitation of diffusion tensor imaging?
options: It cannot be performed on an MRI scanner
The simple tensor model struggles to resolve crossing fibres within a single voxel
It directly images individual axons without any modelling
It provides higher spatial resolution than any other MRI sequence
It is the fastest routine sequence acquired in every brain MRI
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.answer: The simple tensor model struggles to resolve crossing fibres within a single voxel
investigations__MRI__Whole Body / Functi.explanation: A key weakness of DTI is that the single-tensor model cannot faithfully represent multiple fibre populations crossing within one voxel. It is also an indirect, model-based reconstruction (tracts are inferred, not literally imaged) and is a specialised, research-heavy technique requiring dedicated acquisition and post-processing — not a routine sequence.
